title: The Canterbury Tales
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
note: The Canterbury Tales — a full sitting.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: WHEN that Aprilis, with his showers swoot*, *sweet The drought of March hath pierced to the root, And bathed every vein in such licour, Of which virtue engender’d is the flower; When Zephyrus eke with his swoote breath Inspired hath in every holt* and heath *grove, forest The tender croppes* and the younge sun *twigs, boughs Hath in the Ram <1> his halfe course y-run, And smalle fowles make melody, That sleepen all the night with open eye, (So pricketh them nature in their corages*); *hearts, inclinations Then longe folk to go on pilgrimages, And palmers <2> for to seeke strange strands, To *ferne hallows couth* in sundry lands; *distant saints known*<3> And specially, from every shire’s end Of Engleland, to Canterbury they wend, The holy blissful Martyr for to seek, That them hath holpen*, when that they were sick. *helped Befell that, in that season on a day, In Southwark at the Tabard <4> as I lay, Ready to wenden on my pilgrimage To Canterbury with devout corage, At night was come into that hostelry Well nine and twenty in a company Of sundry folk, *by aventure y-fall *who had by chance fallen In fellowship*, and pilgrims were they all, into company.* <5> That toward Canterbury woulde ride.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Tyrwhitt points out that “the Bull” should be read here, not “the Ram,” which would place the time of the pilgrimage in the end of March; whereas, in the Prologue to the Man of Law’s Tale, the date is given as the “eight and twenty day of April, that is messenger to May.”

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Dante, in the “Vita Nuova,” distinguishes three classes of pilgrims: palmieri - palmers who go beyond sea to the East, and often bring back staves of palm-wood; peregrini, who go the shrine of St Jago in Galicia; Romei, who go to Rome.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: “Hallows” survives, in the meaning here given, in All Hallows — All-Saints — day.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: The Tabard — the sign of the inn — was a sleeveless coat, worn by heralds.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: In y-fall,” “y” is a corruption of the Anglo-Saxon “ge” prefixed to participles of verbs.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Alisandre: Alexandria, in Egypt, captured by Pierre de Lusignan, king of Cyprus, in 1365 but abandoned immediately afterwards.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: The knight had been placed at the head of the table, above knights of all nations, in Prussia, whither warriors from all countries were wont to repair, to aid the Teutonic Order in their continual conflicts with their heathen neighbours in “Lettowe” or Lithuania (German.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Algesiras was taken from the Moorish king of Grenada, in 1344: the Earls of Derby and Salisbury took part in the siege.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Ilke: same; compare the Scottish phrase “of that ilk,” that is, of the estate which bears the same name as its owner’s title.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: It was the custom for squires of the highest degree to carve at their fathers’ tables.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Peacock Arrows: Large arrows, with peacocks’ feathers.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: A nut-head: With nut-brown hair; or, round like a nut, the hair being cut short.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Grey eyes appear to have been a mark of female beauty in Chaucer’s time.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: “for the mastery” was applied to medicines in the sense of “sovereign” as we now apply it to a remedy.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: It was fashionable to hang bells on horses’ bridles.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: St. Benedict was the first founder of a spiritual order in the Roman church.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Felix says to Paul, “Too much learning hath made thee mad”.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Limitour: A friar with licence or privilege to beg, or exercise other functions, within a certain district: as, “the limitour of Holderness”.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Farme: rent; that is, he paid a premium for his licence to beg.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: In principio: the first words of Genesis and John, employed in some part of the mass.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Lovedays: meetings appointed for friendly settlement of differences; the business was often followed by sports and feasting.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: He would the sea were kept for any thing: he would for anything that the sea were guarded.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Middleburg, at the mouth of the Scheldt, in Holland; Orwell, a seaport in Essex.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Shields: Crowns, so called from the shields stamped on them; French, “ecu;” Italian, “scudo.”

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Poor scholars at the universities used then to go about begging for money to maintain them and their studies.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Parvis: The portico of St. Paul’s, which lawyers frequented to meet their clients.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: St Julian: The patron saint of hospitality, celebrated for supplying his votaries with good lodging and good cheer.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: The place behind Whitehall, where the king’s hawks were caged was called the Mews.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Many a luce in stew: many a pike in his fish-pond; in those Catholic days, when much fish was eaten, no gentleman’s mansion was complete without a “stew”.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Countour: Probably a steward or accountant in the county court.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Vavasour: A landholder of consequence; holding of a duke, marquis, or earl, and ranking below a baron.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: On the dais: On the raised platform at the end of the hall, where sat at meat or in judgement those high in authority, rank or honour; in our days the worthy craftsmen might have been described as “good platform men”.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: To take precedence over all in going to the evening service of the Church, or to festival meetings, to which it was the fashion to carry rich cloaks or mantles against the homecoming.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: The things the cook could make: “marchand tart”, some now unknown ingredient used in cookery; “galingale,” sweet or long rooted cyprus; “mortrewes”, a rich soup made by stamping flesh in a mortar; “Blanc manger”, not what is now called blancmange; one part of it was the brawn of a capon.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: Lodemanage: pilotage, from Anglo-Saxon “ladman,” a leader, guide, or pilot; hence “lodestar,” “lodestone.”

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: The authors mentioned here were the chief medical textbooks of the middle ages.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: The west of England, especially around Bath, was the seat of the cloth-manufacture, as were Ypres and Ghent (Gaunt) in Flanders.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: Chaucer here satirises the fashion of the time, which piled bulky and heavy waddings on ladies’ heads.

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: Moist; here used in the sense of “new”, as in Latin, “mustum” signifies new wine; and elsewhere Chaucer speaks of “moisty ale”, as opposed to “old”.

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: In Galice at Saint James: at the shrine of St Jago of Compostella in Spain.

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: Gat-toothed: Buck-toothed; goat-toothed, to signify her wantonness; or gap-toothed — with gaps between her teeth.

scenes.title: Chapter 42
scenes.reentry: An endowment to sing masses for the soul of the donor.

scenes.title: Chapter 43
scenes.reentry: A ram was the usual prize at wrestling matches.

scenes.title: Chapter 44
scenes.reentry: Cop: Head; German, “Kopf”.

scenes.title: Chapter 45
scenes.reentry: Nose-thirles: nostrils; from the Anglo-Saxon, “thirlian,” to pierce; hence the word “drill,” to bore.

scenes.title: Chapter 46
scenes.reentry: Goliardais: a babbler and a buffoon; Golias was the founder of a jovial sect called by his name.

scenes.title: Chapter 47
scenes.reentry: The proverb says that every honest miller has a thumb of gold; probably Chaucer means that this one was as honest as his brethren.

scenes.title: Chapter 48
scenes.reentry: A Manciple — Latin, “manceps,” a purchaser or contractor - - was an officer charged with the purchase of victuals for inns of court or colleges.

scenes.title: Chapter 49
scenes.reentry: Reeve: A land-steward; still called “grieve” — Anglo-Saxon, “gerefa” in some parts of Scotland.

scenes.title: Chapter 50
scenes.reentry: Sompnour: summoner; an apparitor, who cited delinquents to appear in ecclesiastical courts.

scenes.title: Chapter 51
scenes.reentry: Questio quid juris: “I ask which law (applies)”; a cant lawLatin phrase.

scenes.title: Chapter 53
scenes.reentry: Significavit: an ecclesiastical writ.

scenes.title: Chapter 54
scenes.reentry: Within his jurisdiction he had at his own pleasure the young people (of both sexes) in the diocese.

scenes.title: Chapter 55
scenes.reentry: Pardoner: a seller of pardons or indulgences.

scenes.title: Chapter 56
scenes.reentry: Newe get: new gait, or fashion; “gait” is still used in this sense in some parts of the country.

scenes.title: Chapter 57
scenes.reentry: Vernicle: an image of Christ; so called from St Veronica, who gave the Saviour a napkin to wipe the sweat from His face as He bore the Cross, and received it back with an impression of His countenance upon it.

scenes.title: Chapter 58
scenes.reentry: Mail: packet, baggage; French, “malle,” a trunk.

scenes.title: Chapter 59
scenes.reentry: The Bell: apparently another Southwark tavern; Stowe mentions a “Bull” as being near the Tabard.

scenes.title: Chapter 60
scenes.reentry: Cheap: Cheapside, then inhabited by the richest and most prosperous citizens of London.

scenes.title: Chapter 61
scenes.reentry: Herberow: Lodging, inn; French, “Herberge.”

scenes.title: Chapter 62
scenes.reentry: The watering of Saint Thomas: At the second milestone on the old Canterbury road.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: For the plan and principal incidents of the “Knight’s Tale,” Chaucer was indebted to Boccaccio, who had himself borrowed from some prior poet, chronicler, or romancer.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Highte: was called; from the Anglo-Saxon “hatan”, to bid or call; German, “Heissen”, “heisst”.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Feminie: The “Royaume des Femmes” — kingdom of the Amazons.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Wonnen: Won, conquered; German “gewonnen.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: The first, and half of the second, of Boccaccio’s twelve books are disposed of in the few lines foregoing.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Waimenting: bewailing; German, “wehklagen”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Starf: died; German, “sterben,” “starb”.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: The Minotaur: The monster, half-man and half-bull, which yearly devoured a tribute of fourteen Athenian youths and maidens, until it was slain by Theseus.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Pillers: pillagers, strippers; French, “pilleurs.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: The donjon was originally the central tower or “keep” of feudal castles; it was employed to detain prisoners of importance.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Saturn, in the old astrology, was a most unpropitious star to be born under.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: To die in the pain was a proverbial expression in the French, used as an alternative to enforce a resolution or a promise.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: The saying of the old scholar Boethius, in his treatise “De Consolatione Philosophiae”, which Chaucer translated, and from which he has freely borrowed in his poetry.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: “Perithous” and “Theseus” must, for the metre, be pronounced as words of four and three syllables respectively the vowels at the end not being diphthongated, but enunciated separately, as if the words were printed Pe-ri-tho-us, The-se-us.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Stound: moment, short space of time; from Anglo-Saxon, “stund;” akin to which is German, “Stunde,” an hour.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Meinie: servants, or menials, &c., dwelling together in a house; from an Anglo-Saxon word meaning a crowd.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: The Greeks used “katharos”, the Romans “purus,” in the same sense.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: In the medieval courts of Love, to which allusion is probably made forty lines before, in the word “parlement,” or “parliament,” questions like that here proposed were seriously discussed.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Gear: behaviour, fashion, dress; but, by another reading, the word is “gyre,” and means fit, trance — from the Latin, “gyro,” I turn round.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Before his head in his cell fantastic: in front of his head in his cell of fantasy.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Dan: Lord; Latin, “Dominus;” Spanish, “Don.”

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Argus was employed by Juno to watch Io with his hundred eyes but he was sent to sleep by the flute of Mercury, who then cut off his head.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Next: nearest; German, “naechste”.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Clary: hippocras, wine made with spices.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Warray: make war; French “guerroyer”, to molest; hence, perhaps, “to worry.”

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: All day meeten men at unset steven: every day men meet at unexpected time.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Roundelay: song coming round again to the words with which it opened.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Now in the crop and now down in the breres: Now in the tree-top, now down in the briars.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Beknow: avow, acknowledge: German, “bekennen.”

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Shapen was my death erst than my shert: My death was decreed before my shirt ws shaped — that is, before any clothes were made for me, before my birth.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: Regne: Queen; French, “Reine;” Venus is meant.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Compare modern English, “lawn,” and French, “Landes” — flat, bare marshy tracts in the south of France.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: Mister: manner, kind; German “muster,” sample, model.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: In listes: in the lists, prepared for such single combats between champion and accuser, &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: Thilke: that, contracted from “the ilke,” the same.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: Mars the Red: referring to the ruddy colour of the planet, to which was doubtless due the transference to it of the name of the God of War.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: Last: lace, leash, noose, snare: from Latin, “laceus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: “Round was the shape, in manner of compass, Full of degrees, the height of sixty pas” The building was a circle of steps or benches, as in the ancient amphitheatre.

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: Yellow goldes: The sunflower, turnsol, or girasol, which turns with and seems to watch the sun, as a jealous lover his mistress.

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: Citheron: The Isle of Venus, Cythera, in the Aegean Sea; now called Cerigo: not, as Chaucer’s form of the word might imply, Mount Cithaeron, in the south-west of Boetia, which was appropriated to other deities than Venus — to Jupiter, to Bacchus, and the Muses.

scenes.title: Chapter 42
scenes.reentry: It need not be said that Chaucer pays slight heed to chronology in this passage, where the deeds of Turnus, the glory of King Solomon, and the fate of Croesus are made memories of the far past in the time of fabulous Theseus, the Minotaur-slayer.

scenes.title: Chapter 43
scenes.reentry: Champartie: divided power or possession; an old law-term, signifying the maintenance of a person in a law suit on the condition of receiving part of the property in dispute, if recovered.

scenes.title: Chapter 44
scenes.reentry: Citole: a kind of dulcimer.

scenes.title: Chapter 45
scenes.reentry: The picke-purse: The plunderers that followed armies, and gave to war a horror all their own.

scenes.title: Chapter 46
scenes.reentry: Shepen: stable; Anglo-Saxon, “scypen;” the word “sheppon” still survives in provincial parlance.

scenes.title: Chapter 47
scenes.reentry: This line, perhaps, refers to the deed of Jael.

scenes.title: Chapter 48
scenes.reentry: The shippes hoppesteres: The meaning is dubious.

scenes.title: Chapter 49
scenes.reentry: Freting: devouring; the Germans use “Fressen” to mean eating by animals, “essen” by men.

scenes.title: Chapter 51
scenes.reentry: Puella and Rubeus were two figures in geomancy, representing two constellations-the one signifying Mars retrograde, the other Mars direct.

scenes.title: Chapter 52
scenes.reentry: Calistope: or Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, seduced by Jupiter, turned into a bear by Diana, and placed afterwards, with her son, as the Great Bear among the stars.

scenes.title: Chapter 53
scenes.reentry: Dane: Daphne, daughter of the river-god Peneus, in Thessaly; she was beloved by Apollo, but to avoid his pursuit, she was, at her own prayer, changed into a laurel-tree.

scenes.title: Chapter 54
scenes.reentry: As the goddess of Light, or the goddess who brings to light, Diana — as well as Juno — was invoked by women in childbirth: so Horace, Odes iii.

scenes.title: Chapter 55
scenes.reentry: Every deal: in every part; “deal” corresponds to the German “Theil” a portion.

scenes.title: Chapter 56
scenes.reentry: Sikerly: surely; German, “sicher;” Scotch, “sikkar,” certain.

scenes.title: Chapter 57
scenes.reentry: Kemped: combed; the word survives in “unkempt.”

scenes.title: Chapter 58
scenes.reentry: Alauns: greyhounds, mastiffs; from the Spanish word “Alano,” signifying a mastiff.

scenes.title: Chapter 59
scenes.reentry: Y-ment: mixed; German, “mengen,” to mix.

scenes.title: Chapter 60
scenes.reentry: Prime: The time of early prayers, between six and nine in the morning.

scenes.title: Chapter 61
scenes.reentry: On the dais: see note 32 to the Prologue.

scenes.title: Chapter 62
scenes.reentry: In her hour: in the hour of the day (two hours before daybreak) which after the astrological system that divided the twenty-four among the seven ruling planets, was under the influence of Venus.

scenes.title: Chapter 63
scenes.reentry: Adon: Adonis, a beautiful youth beloved of Venus, whose death by the tusk of a boar she deeply mourned.

scenes.title: Chapter 64
scenes.reentry: The third hour unequal: In the third planetary hour; Palamon had gone forth in the hour of Venus, two hours before daybreak; the hour of Mercury intervened; the third hour was that of Luna, or Diana.

scenes.title: Chapter 65
scenes.reentry: Smoking: draping; hence the word “smock;” “smokless,” in Chaucer, means naked.

scenes.title: Chapter 66
scenes.reentry: Cerrial: of the species of oak which Pliny, in his “Natural History,” calls “cerrus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 67
scenes.reentry: Stace of Thebes: Statius, the Roman who embodied in the twelve books of his “Thebaid” the ancient legends connected with the war of the seven against Thebes.

scenes.title: Chapter 68
scenes.reentry: Diana was Luna in heaven, Diana on earth, and Hecate in hell; hence the direction of the eyes of her statue to “Pluto’s dark region.”

scenes.title: Chapter 69
scenes.reentry: Las: net; the invisible toils in which Hephaestus caught Ares and the faithless Aphrodite, and exposed them to the “inextinguishable laughter” of Olympus.

scenes.title: Chapter 70
scenes.reentry: Saturnus the cold: Here, as in “Mars the Red” we have the person of the deity endowed with the supposed quality of the planet called after his name.

scenes.title: Chapter 71
scenes.reentry: The astrologers ascribed great power to Saturn, and predicted “much debate” under his ascendancy; hence it was “against his kind” to compose the heavenly strife.

scenes.title: Chapter 72
scenes.reentry: Ayel: grandfather; French “Aieul”.

scenes.title: Chapter 73
scenes.reentry: Testers: Helmets; from the French “teste”, “tete”, head.

scenes.title: Chapter 74
scenes.reentry: Parements: ornamental garb, French “parer” to deck.

scenes.title: Chapter 75
scenes.reentry: Gniding: Rubbing, polishing; Anglo-Saxon “gnidan”, to rub.

scenes.title: Chapter 76
scenes.reentry: Nakeres: Drums, used in the cavalry; Boccaccio’s word is “nachere”.

scenes.title: Chapter 77
scenes.reentry: Ho! to command attention; like “oyez”, the call for silence in law-courts or before proclamations.

scenes.title: Chapter 78
scenes.reentry: Sarge: serge, a coarse woollen cloth

scenes.title: Chapter 79
scenes.reentry: Heart-spoon: The concave part of the breast, where the lower ribs join the cartilago ensiformis.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Pilate, an unpopular personage in the mystery-plays of the middle ages, was probably represented as having a gruff, harsh voice.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Wite: blame; in Scotland, “to bear the wyte,” is to bear the blame.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Almagest: The book of Ptolemy the astronomer, which formed the canon of astrological science in the middle ages.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Astrolabe: “Astrelagour,” “astrelabore”; a mathematical instrument for taking the altitude of the sun or stars.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: “Augrim” is a corruption of algorithm, the Arabian term for numeration; “augrim stones,” therefore were probably marked with numerals, and used as counters.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Angelus ad virginem: The Angel’s salutation to Mary; Luke i.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: It was the “Ave Maria” of the Catholic Church service.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Cato: Though Chaucer may have referred to the famous Censor, more probably the reference is merely to the “Moral Distichs,” which go under his name, though written after his time; and in a supplement to which the quoted passage may be found.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Barm-cloth: apron; from Anglo-Saxon “barme,” bosom or lap.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Volupere: Head-gear, kerchief; from French, “envelopper,” to wrap up.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Popelet: Puppet; but chiefly; young wench.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Noble: nobles were gold coins of especial purity and brightness; “Ex auro nobilissimi, unde nobilis vocatus,” (made from the noblest (purest) gold, and therefore called nobles) says Vossius.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Yern: Shrill, lively; German, “gern,” willingly, cheerfully.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Braket: bragget, a sweet drink made of honey, spices, &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Piggesnie: a fond term, like “my duck;” from Anglo-Saxon, “piga,” a young maid; but Tyrwhitt associates it with the Latin, “ocellus,” little eye, a fondling term, and suggests that the “pigseye,” which is very small, was applied in the same sense.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Oseney: A once well-known abbey near Oxford.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Trave: travis; a frame in which unruly horses were shod.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Harow and Alas: Haro! was an old Norman cry for redress or aid.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: His shoes were ornamented like the windows of St. Paul’s, especially like the old rose-window.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Rise: Twig, bush; German, “Reis,” a twig; “Reisig,” a copse.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Chaucer satirises the dancing of Oxford as he did the French of Stratford at Bow.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Shot window: A projecting or bow window, whence it was possible shoot at any one approaching the door.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Piment: A drink made with wine, honey, and spices.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Because she was town-bred, he offered wealth, or money reward, for her love.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Parish-clerks, like Absolon, had leading parts in the mysteries or religious plays; Herod was one of these parts, which may have been an object of competition among the amateurs of the period.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Kyked: Looked; “keek” is still used in some parts in the sense of “peep.”

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Saint Frideswide was the patroness of a considerable priory at Oxford, and held there in high repute.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Plato, in his “Theatetus,” tells this story of Thales; but it has since appeared in many other forms.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Crouche: protect by signing the sign of the cross.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Forlore: lost; german, “verloren.”

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Him that harried Hell: Christ who wasted or subdued hell: in the middle ages, some very active exploits against the prince of darkness and his powers were ascribed by the monkish taletellers to the saviour after he had “descended into hell.”

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: According to the old mysteries, Noah’s wife refused to come into the ark, and bade her husband row forth and get him a new wife, because he was leaving her gossips in the town to drown.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: “Him had been lever, I dare well undertake, At thilke time, than all his wethers black, That she had had a ship herself alone.” i.e.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: “Clum,” like “mum,” a note of silence; but otherwise explained as the humming sound made in repeating prayers; from the Anglo-Saxon, “clumian,” to mutter, speak in an undertone, keep silence.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Curfew-time: Eight in the evening, when, by the law of William the Conqueror, all people were, on ringing of a bell, to extinguish fire and candle, and go to rest; hence the word curfew, from French, “couvre-feu,” cover-fire.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: Absolon chewed grains: these were grains of Paris, or Paradise; a favourite spice.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: Under his tongue a true love he bare: some sweet herb; another reading, however, is “a true love-knot,” which may have been of the nature of a charm.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: The two lines within brackets are not in most of the editions: they are taken from Urry; whether he supplied them or not, they serve the purpose of a necessary explanation.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: Gay girl: As applied to a young woman of light manners, this euphemistic phrase has enjoyed a wonderful vitality.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: Viretote: Urry reads “meritote,” and explains it from Spelman as a game in which children made themselves giddy by whirling on ropes.

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: He had more tow on his distaff: a proverbial saying: he was playing a deeper game, had more serious business on hand.

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: Ere: before; German, “eher.”

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: Sell: sill of the door, threshold; French, “seuil,” Latin, “solum,” the ground.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: “With blearing of a proude miller’s eye”: dimming his eye; playing off a joke on him.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: “Me list not play for age”: age takes away my zest for drollery.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: The medlar, the fruit of the mespilus tree, is only edible when rotten.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Yet in our ashes cold does fire reek: “ev’n in our ashes live their wonted fires.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: A colt’s tooth; a wanton humour, a relish for pleasure.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Chimb: The rim of a barrel where the staves project beyond the head.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: With olde folk, save dotage, is no more: Dotage is all that is left them; that is, they can only dwell fondly, dote, on the past.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Souter: cobbler; Scottice, “sutor;”’ from Latin, “suere,” to sew.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: “Ex sutore medicus” (a surgeon from a cobbler) and “ex sutore nauclerus” (a seaman or pilot from a cobbler) were both proverbial expressions in the Middle Ages.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Half past prime: half-way between prime and tierce; about half-past seven in the morning.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Set his hove; like “set their caps;” as in the description of the Manciple in the Prologue, who “set their aller cap”.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: The illustration of the mote and the beam, from Matthew.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The incidents of this tale were much relished in the Middle Ages, and are found under various forms.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Camuse: flat; French “camuse”, snub-nosed.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Gite: gown or coat; French “jupe.”

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Soler Hall: the hall or college at Cambridge with the gallery or upper storey; supposed to have been Clare Hall.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Manciple: steward; provisioner of the hall.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Testif: headstrong, wild-brained; French, “entete.”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Strother: Tyrwhitt points to Anstruther, in Fife: Mr Wright to the Vale of Langstroth, in the West Riding of Yorkshire.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Wanges: grinders, cheek-teeth; Anglo-Saxon, “Wang,” the cheek; German, “Wange.”

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: See note 1 to the Prologue to the Reeves Tale

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: In the “Cento Novelle Antiche,” the story is told of a mule, which pretends that his name is written on the bottom of his hind foot.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Levesell: an arbour; Anglo-Saxon, “lefe-setl,” leafy seat.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Noth: business; German, “Noth,” necessity.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Bathe: both; Scottice, “baith.”

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Capel: horse; Gaelic, “capall;” French, “cheval;” Italian, “cavallo,” from Latin, “caballus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Make a clerkes beard: cheat a scholar; French, “faire la barbe;” and Boccaccio uses the proverb in the same sense.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: “Gar” is Scotch for “cause;” some editions read, however, “get us some”.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Chalons: blankets, coverlets, made at Chalons in France.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Crock: pitcher, cruse; Anglo-Saxon, “crocca;” German, “krug;” hence “crockery.”

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Dwale: night-shade, Solanum somniferum, given to cause sleep.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: It originally means the drone of a bagpipe; French, “bourdon.”

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Compline: even-song in the church service; chorus.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: In Scotland, a “ferlie” is an unwonted or remarkable sight.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: A furlong way: As long as it might take to walk a furlong.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Cockenay: a term of contempt, probably borrowed from the kitchen; a cook, in base Latin, being termed “coquinarius.” compare French “coquin,” rascal.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Unhardy is unsely: the cowardly is unlucky; “nothing venture, nothing have;” German, “unselig,” unhappy.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Holy cross of Bromeholm: A common adjuration at that time; the cross or rood of the priory of Bromholm, in Norfolk, was said to contain part of the real cross and therefore held in high esteem.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: THE Cook of London, while the Reeve thus spake, For joy he laugh’d and clapp’d him on the back: “Aha!” quoth he, “for Christes passion, This Miller had a sharp conclusion, Upon this argument of herbergage.* *lodging Well saide Solomon in his language, Bring thou not every man into thine house, For harbouring by night is perilous. *Well ought a man avised for to be* *a man should take good heed* Whom that he brought into his privity.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Jack of Dover: an article of cookery.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Sooth play quad play: true jest is no jest.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: It may be remembered that each pilgrim was bound to tell two stories; one on the way to Canterbury, the other returning.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Made cheer: French, “fit bonne mine;” put on a pleasant countenance.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Cheapside, where jousts were sometimes held, and which was the great scene of city revels and processions.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: His paper: his certificate of completion of his apprenticeship.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Louke: The precise meaning of the word is unknown, but it is doubtless included in the cant term “pal”.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: The Cook’s Tale is unfinished in all the manuscripts; but in some, of minor authority, the Cook is made to break off his tale, because “it is so foul,” and to tell the story of Gamelyn, on which Shakespeare’s “As You Like It” is founded.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Plight: pulled; the word is an obsolete past tense from “pluck.”

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: No more than will Malkin’s maidenhead: a proverbial saying; which, however, had obtained fresh point from the Reeve’s Tale, to which the host doubtless refers.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: De par dieux jeo asente: “by God, I agree”.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Ceyx and Alcyon: Chaucer treats of these in the introduction to the poem called “The Book of the Duchess.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: The Saintes Legend of Cupid: Now called “The Legend of Good Women”.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Not the Muses, who had their surname from the place near Mount Olympus where the Thracians first worshipped them; but the nine daughters of Pierus, king of Macedonia, whom he called the nine Muses, and who, being conquered in a contest with the genuine sisterhood, were changed into birds.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Metamorphoseos: Ovid’s.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Hawebake: hawbuck, country lout; the common proverbial phrase, “to put a rogue above a gentleman,” may throw light on the reading here, which is difficult.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: This tale is believed by Tyrwhitt to have been taken, with no material change, from the “Confessio Amantis” of John Gower, who was contemporary with Chaucer, though somewhat his senior.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Transcriber’ note: This refers to the game of hazard, a dice game like craps, in which two (“ambes ace”) won, and eleven (“six-cinque”) lost.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Purpose: discourse, tale: French “propos”.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: “Peace” rhymed with “lese” and “chese”, the old forms of “lose” and “choose”.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: According to Middle Age writers there were two motions of the first heaven; one everything always from east to west above the stars; the other moving the stars against the first motion, from west to east, on two other poles.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Atyzar: the meaning of this word is not known; but “occifer”, murderer, has been suggested instead by Urry, on the authority of a marginal reading on a manuscript.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: “Thou knittest thee where thou art not receiv’d, Where thou wert well, from thennes art thou weiv’d” i.e.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Fand: endeavour; from Anglo-Saxon, “fandian,” to try

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Feng: take; Anglo-Saxon “fengian”, German, “fangen”.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Him and her on which thy limbes faithfully extend: those who in faith wear the crucifix.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: The four spirits of tempest: the four angels who held the four winds of the earth and to whom it was given to hurt the earth and the sea (Rev. vii.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Thennes would it not in all a tide: thence would it not move for long, at all.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: A manner Latin corrupt: a kind of bastard Latin.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Knave child: male child; German “Knabe”.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Heried: honoured, praised; from Anglo-Saxon, “herian.”

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Beknow: confess; German, “bekennen.”

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: The poet here refers to Gower’s version of the story.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Stound: short time; German, “stunde”, hour.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Gestes: histories, exploits; Latin, “res gestae”.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Among the evidences that Chaucer’s great work was left incomplete, is the absence of any link of connexion between the Wife of Bath’s Prologue and Tale, and what goes before.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: A great part of the marriage service used to be performed in the church-porch.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Jesus and the Samaritan woman: John iv.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Another reading is “the wise man, King Solomon.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Defended: forbade; French, “defendre,” to prohibit.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Dart: the goal; a spear or dart was set up to mark the point of victory.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.” — 2 Tim. ii 20.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Jesus feeding the multitude with barley bread: Mark vi.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: At Dunmow prevailed the custom of giving, amid much merry making, a flitch of bacon to the married pair who had lived together for a year without quarrel or regret.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: “Cagnard,” or “Caignard,” a French term of reproach, originally derived from “canis,” a dog.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Parage: birth, kindred; from Latin, “pario,” I beget.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Norice: nurse; French, “nourrice.”

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: This and the previous quotation from Ptolemy are due to the Dame’s own fancy.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: The word given in [brackets] should be “queint” i.e. “cunt”.)

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Women should not adorn themselves: see I Tim. ii.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Cherte: affection; from French, “cher,” dear.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Nicety: folly; French, “niaiserie.”

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Ba: kiss; from French, “baiser.”

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Peter!: by Saint Peter! a common adjuration, like Marie! from the Virgin’s name.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: St. Joce: or Judocus, a saint of Ponthieu, in France.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: “An allusion,” says Mr Wright, “to the story of the Roman sage who, when blamed for divorcing his wife, said that a shoe might appear outwardly to fit well, but no one but the wearer knew where it pinched.”

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Vigilies: festival-eves; see note 33 to the Prologue to the Tales.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Bobance: boasting; Ben Jonson’s braggart, in “Every Man in his Humour,” is named Bobadil.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: “I hold a mouse’s wit not worth a leek, That hath but one hole for to starte to” A very old proverb in French, German, and Latin.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: The lines in brackets are only in some of the manuscripts.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Gat-toothed: gap-toothed; goat-toothed; or cator separate toothed.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Sempronius Sophus, of whom Valerius Maximus tells in his sixth book.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: The tract of Walter Mapes against marriage, published under the title of “Epistola Valerii ad Rufinum.”

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: All the mark of Adam: all who bear the mark of Adam i.e. all men.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: The Children of Mercury and Venus: those born under the influence of the respective planets.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: A planet, according to the old astrologers, was in “exaltation” when in the sign of the Zodiac in which it exerted its strongest influence; the opposite sign, in which it was weakest, was called its “dejection.”

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Intermete: interpose; French, “entremettre.”

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: It is not clear whence Chaucer derived this tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: See note 18 to the prologue to the Tales.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Thorpes: villages.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Undermeles: evening-tides, afternoons; “undern” signifies the evening; and “mele,” corresponds to the German “Mal” or “Mahl,” time.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Incubus: an evil spirit supposed to do violence to women; a nightmare.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Where he had been hawking after waterfowl.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Nice: foolish; French, “niais.”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Claw us on the gall: Scratch us on the sore place.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Hele: hide; from Anglo-Saxon, “helan,” to hide, conceal.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Yern: eagerly; German, “gern.”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Wiss: instruct; German, “weisen,” to show or counsel.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Dante, “Purgatorio”, vii.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: “Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator” — “Satires,” x.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: In a fabulous conference between the Emperor Adrian and the philosopher Secundus, reported by Vincent of Beauvais, occurs the passage which Chaucer here paraphrases: — “Quid est Paupertas?

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Elenge: strange; from French “eloigner,” to remove.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: On the Tale of the Friar, and that of the Sompnour which follows, Tyrwhitt has remarked that they “are well engrafted upon that of the Wife of Bath.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Small tithers: people who did not pay their full tithes.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: There might astert them no pecunial pain: they got off with no mere pecuniary punishment.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: A dog for the bow: a dog attending a huntsman with bow and arrow.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Ribibe: the name of a musical instrument; applied to an old woman because of the shrillness of her voice.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: De par dieux: by the gods.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: See note 12 to the Knight’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Wariangles: butcher-birds; which are very noisy and ravenous, and tear in pieces the birds on which they prey; the thorn on which they do this was said to become poisonous.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Medieval legends located hell in the North.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: The Pythoness: the witch, or woman, possesed with a prophesying spirit; from the Greek, “Pythia.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Dante and Virgil were both poets who had in fancy visited Hell.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Tholed: suffered, endured; “thole” is still used in Scotland in the same sense.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Capels: horses.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Liart: grey; elsewhere applied by Chaucer to the hairs of an old man.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Rebeck: a kind of fiddle; used like “ribibe,” as a nickname for a shrill old scold.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Trot; a contemptuous term for an old woman who has trotted about much, or who moves with quick short steps.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: In his await: on the watch; French, “aux aguets.”

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Carrack: A great ship of burden used by the Portuguese; the name is from the Italian, “cargare,” to load

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: In less than half a furlong way of space: immediately; literally, in less time than it takes to walk half a furlong (110 yards).

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Trentals: The money given to the priests for performing thirty masses for the dead, either in succession or on the anniversaries of their death; also the masses themselves, which were very profitable to the clergy.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Possessioners: The regular religious orders, who had lands and fixed revenues; while the friars, by their vows, had to depend on voluntary contributions, though their need suggested many modes of evading the prescription.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: In Chaucer’s day the most material notions about the tortures of hell prevailed, and were made the most of by the clergy, who preyed on the affection and fear of the survivors, through the ingenious doctrine of purgatory.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Qui cum patre: “Who with the father”; the closing words of the final benediction pronounced at Mass.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Askaunce: The word now means sideways or asquint; here it means “as if;” and its force is probably to suggest that the second friar, with an ostentatious stealthiness, noted down the names of the liberal, to make them believe that they would be remembered in the holy beggars’ orisons.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: A Godde’s kichel/halfpenny: a little cake/halfpenny, given for God’s sake.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Harlot: hired servant; from Anglo-Saxon, “hyran,” to hire; the word was commonly applied to males.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Potent: staff; French, “potence,” crutch, gibbet.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Je vous dis sans doute: French; “I tell you without doubt.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Dortour: dormitory; French, “dortoir.”

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: The Rules of St Benedict granted peculiar honours and immunities to monks who had lived fifty years — the jubilee period — in the order.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Borel folk: laymen, people who are not learned; “borel” was a kind of coarse cloth.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Eli: Elijah (1 Kings, xix.)

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: An emperor Jovinian was famous in the mediaeval legends for his pride and luxury

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: 1.). “Buf” is meant to represent the sound of an eructation, and to show the “great reverence” with which “those in possession,” the monks of the rich monasteries, performed divine service,

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: N’ere thou our brother, shouldest thou not thrive: if thou wert not of our brotherhood, thou shouldst have no hope of recovery.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Thomas’ life of Ind: The life of Thomas of India - i.e.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Potestate: chief magistrate or judge; Latin, “potestas;” Italian, “podesta.”

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Placebo: An anthem of the Roman Church, from Psalm cxvi.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: The Gysen: Seneca calls it the Gyndes; Sir John Mandeville tells the story of the Euphrates.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Him that harrowed Hell: Christ.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Mr. Wright says that “it was a common practice to grant under the conventual seal to benefactors and others a brotherly participation in the spiritual good works of the convent, and in their expected reward after death.”

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: The friar had received a master’s degree.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: The regular number of monks or friars in a convent was fixed at twelve, with a superior, in imitation of the apostles and their Master; and large religious houses were held to consist of so many convents.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Under your yerd: under your rod; as the emblem of government or direction.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Francesco Petrarca, born 1304, died 1374; for his Latin epic poem on the carer of Scipio, called “Africa,” he was solemnly crowned with the poetic laurel in the Capitol of Rome, on Easter-day of 1341.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Linian: An eminent jurist and philosopher, now almost forgotten, who died four or five years after Petrarch.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Saluces: Saluzzo, a district of Savoy; its marquises were celebrated during the Middle Ages.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Emilia: The region called Aemilia, across which ran the Via Aemilia — made by M. Aemilius Lepidus, who was consul at Rome B.C.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Petrarch, in his Latin romance, “De obedientia et fide uxoria Mythologia,” (Of obedient and faithful wives in Mythology) translated the charming story of “the patient Grizel” from the Italian of Bocaccio’s “Decameron;” and Chaucer has closely followed Petrarch’s translation, made in 1373, the year before that in which he died.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Vesulus: Monte Viso, a lofty peak at the junction of the Maritime and Cottian Alps; from two springs on its east side rises the Po.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Buxomly: obediently; Anglo-Saxon, “bogsom,” old English, “boughsome,” that can be easily bent or bowed; German, “biegsam,” pliant, obedient.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Well ofter of the well than of the tun she drank: she drank water much more often than wine.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Undern: afternoon, evening, though by some “undern” is understood as dinner-time — 9 a. m.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Very: true; French “vrai”.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Nouches: Ornaments of some kind not precisely known; some editions read “ouches,” studs, brooches.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: A furlong way or two: a short time; literally, as long as it takes to walk one or two furlongs (a furlong is 220 yards)

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Lordes’ hestes may not be y-feign’d: it will not do merely to feign compliance with a lord’s commands.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Arace: tear; French, “arracher.”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Fele: many; German, “viel.”

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: A jane was a small coin of little worth, so the meaning is “not worth a red cent”.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Mo: me. “This is one of the most licentious corruptions of orthography,” says Tyrwhitt, “that I remember to have observed in Chaucer;” but such liberties were common among the European poets of his time, when there was an extreme lack of certainty in orthography.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: The fourteen lines that follow are translated almost literally from Petrarch’s Latin.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: For great skill is he proved that he wrought: for it is most reasonable that He should prove or test that which he made.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Chichevache, in old popular fable, was a monster that fed only on good women, and was always very thin from scarcity of such food; a corresponding monster, Bycorne, fed only on obedient and kind husbands, and was always fat.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Countertail: Counter-tally or counter-foil; something exactly corresponding.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: “Weeping and wailing, care and other sorrow, I have enough, on even and on morrow,” Quoth the Merchant, “and so have other mo’, That wedded be; I trow* that it be so; *believe For well I wot it fareth so by me.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Though the manner in which the Merchant takes up the closing words of the Envoy to the Clerk’s Tale, and refers to the patience of Griselda, seems to prove beyond doubt that the order of the Tales in the text is the right one, yet in some manuscripts of good authority the Franklin’s Tale follows the Clerk’s, and the Envoy is concluded by this stanza: — “This worthy Clerk when ended was his tale, Our Hoste said, and swore by cocke’s bones ‘Me lever were than a barrel of ale My wife at home had heard this legend once; This is a gentle tale for the nonce; As, to my purpose, wiste ye my will.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Saint Thomas of Ind: St. Thomas the Apostle, who was believed to have travelled in India.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: If, as is probable, this Tale was translated from the French, the original is not now extant.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Seculeres: of the laity; but perhaps, since the word is of twofold meaning, Chaucer intends a hit at the secular clergy, who, unlike the regular orders, did not live separate from the world, but shared in all its interests and pleasures — all the more easily and freely, that they had not the civil restraint of marriage.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: This and the next eight lines are taken from the “Liber aureolus Theophrasti de nuptiis,” (“Theophrastus’s Golden Book of Marriage”) quoted by Hieronymus, “Contra Jovinianum,” (“Against Jovinian”) and thence again by John of Salisbury.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Mebles: movables, furniture, &c.; French, “meubles.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “Wade’s boat” was called Guingelot; and in it, according to the old romance, the owner underwent a long series of wild adventures, and performed many strange exploits.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Stopen: advanced; past participle of “step.”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: They did not need to go in quest of a wife for him, as they had promised.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Thilke tree: that tree of original sin, of which the special sins are the branches.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Skinked: poured out; from Anglo-Saxon, “scencan.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Marcianus Capella, who wrote a kind of philosophical romance, “De Nuptiis Mercurii et Philologiae” (Of the Marriage of Mercury and Philology) .

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Familiar: domestic; belonging to the “familia,” or household.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Hewe: domestic servant; from Anglo-Saxon, “hiwa.”

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Boren man: born; owing to January faith and loyalty because born in his household.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Vernage: a wine believed to have come from Crete, although its name — Italian, “Vernaccia” — seems to be derived from Verona.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Dan Constantine: a medical author who wrote about 1080; his works were printed at Basle in 1536.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Full of jargon as a flecked pie: he chattered like a magpie

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Nearly all the manuscripts read “in two of Taure;” but Tyrwhitt has shown that, setting out from the second degree of Taurus, the moon, which in the four complete days that Maius spent in her chamber could not have advanced more than fiftythree degrees, would only have been at the twenty-fifth degree of Gemini — whereas, by reading “ten,” she is brought to the third degree of Cancer.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Kid; or “kidde,” past participle of “kythe” or “kithe,” to show or discover.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Precious: precise, over-nice; French, “precieux,” affected.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Proined: or “pruned;” carefully trimmed and dressed himself.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: A dogge for the bow: a dog attending a hunter with the bow.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Priapus: Son of Bacchus and Venus: he was regarded as the promoter of fertility in all agricultural life, vegetable and animal; while not only gardens, but fields, flocks, bees — and even fisheries — were supposed to be under his protection.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Argus was employed by Juno to watch Io with his hundred eyes but he was sent to sleep by the flute of Mercury, who then cut off his head.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: “My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: “That fair field, Of Enna, where Proserpine, gath’ring flowers, Herself a fairer flow’r, by gloomy Dis Was gather’d.” — Milton, Paradise Lost, iv.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: “Behold, this have I found, saith the preacher, counting one by one, to find out the account: Which yet my soul seeketh, but I find not: one man amongst a thousand have I found, but a woman among all those I have not found.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Jesus, the son of Sirach, to whom is ascribed one of the books of the Apochrypha — that called the “Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus;” in which, especially in the ninth and twenty-fifth chapters, severe cautions are given against women.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Roman gestes: histories; such as those of Lucretia, Porcia, &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: May means January to believe that she is pregnant, and that she has a craving for unripe pears.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: At this point, and again some twenty lines below, several verses of a very coarse character had been inserted in later manuscripts; but they are evidently spurious, and are omitted in the best editions.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: “Store” is the general reading here, but its meaning is not obvious.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Women connen utter such chaffare: women are adepts at giving circulation to such wares.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Squire’s Tale has not been found under any other form among the literary remains of the Middle Ages; and it is unknown from what original it was derived, if from any.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: The Russians and Tartars waged constant hostilities between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: In the best manuscripts the name is “Cambynskan,” and thus, no doubt, it should strictly be read.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Couth his colours longing for that art: well skilled in using the colours — the word-painting — belonging to his art.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Aries was the mansion of Mars — to whom “his” applies.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: The precise force of the word is uncertain; but it may be connected with “seethe,” to boil, and it seems to describe a dish in which the flesh was served up amid a kind of broth or gravy.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Heronsews: young herons; French, “heronneaux.”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Purpose: story, discourse; French, “propos.”

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Gawain was celebrated in mediaeval romance as the most courteous among King Arthur’s knights.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Compare Italian, “inganno,” deception; and our own “engine.”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Mr Wright remarks that “the making and arrangement of seals was one of the important operations of mediaeval magic.”

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Remued: removed; French, “remuer,” to stir.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: The horses of Apulia — in old French “Poille,” in Italian “Puglia” — were held in high value.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: The Greeke’s horse Sinon: the wooden horse of the Greek Sinon, introduced into Troy by the stratagem of its maker.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Master tower: chief tower; as, in the Knight’s Tale, the principal street is called the “master street.”

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Alhazen and Vitellon: two writers on optics — the first supposed to have lived about 1100, the other about 1270.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Telephus, a son of Hercules, reigned over Mysia when the Greeks came to besiege Troy, and he sought to prevent their landing.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Ferne: before; a corruption of “forne,” from Anglo-Saxon, “foran.”

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Aldrian: or Aldebaran; a star in the neck of the constellation Leo.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Chamber of parements: Presence-chamber, or chamber of state, full of splendid furniture and ornaments.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: In Pisces, Venus was said to be at her exaltation or greatest power.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Launcelot: Arthur’s famous knight, so accomplished and courtly, that he was held the very pink of chivalry.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Trill: turn; akin to “thirl”, “drill.”

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Ride: another reading is “bide,” alight or remain.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Feastying: entertaining; French, “festoyer,” to feast.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: The old physicians held that blood dominated in the human body late at night and in the early morning.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Fumosity: fumes of wine rising from the stomach to the head.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Fremde: foreign, strange; German, “fremd” in the northern dialects, “frem,” or “fremmed,” is used in the same sense.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Leden: Language, dialect; from Anglo-Saxon, “leden” or “laeden,” a corruption from “Latin.”

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Tercelet: the “tassel,” or male of any species of hawk; so called, according to Cotgrave, because he is one third (“tiers”) smaller than the female.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: “And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Gen. iv.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: Galoche: shoe; it seems to have been used in France, of a “sabot,” or wooden shoe.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Byleve; stay; another form is “bleve;” from Anglo-Saxon, “belitan,” to remain.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: This sentiment, as well as the illustration of the bird which follows, is taken from the third book of Boethius, “De Consolatione Philosophiae,” metrum 2.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: Men love of proper kind newfangleness: Men, by their own — their very — nature, are fond of novelty, and prone to inconstancy.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: Blue was the colour of truth, as green was that of inconstancy.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: Unless we suppose this to be a namesake of the Camballo who was Canace’s brother — which is not at all probable — we must agree with Tyrwhitt that there is a mistake here; which no doubt Chaucer would have rectified, if the tale had not been “left half-told,” One manuscript reads “Caballo;” and though not much authority need be given to a difference that may be due to mere omission of the mark of contraction over the “a,” there is enough in the text to show that another person than the king’s younger son is intended.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: (Trancriber’s note) In some manuscripts the following two lines, being the beginning of the third part, are found: Apollo whirleth up his chair so high, Till that Mercurius’ house, the sly…

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: In the older editions, the verses here given as the prologue were prefixed to the Merchant’s Tale, and put into his mouth.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: The “Breton Lays” were an important and curious element in the literature of the Middle Ages; they were originally composed in the Armorican language, and the chief collection of them extant was translated into French verse by a poetess calling herself “Marie,” about the middle of the thirteenth century.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Well unnethes durst this knight for dread: This knight hardly dared, for fear (that she would not entertain his suit.)

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: “Ne woulde God never betwixt us twain, As in my guilt, were either war or strife” Would to God there may never be war or strife between us, through my fault.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Perhaps the true reading is “beteth” — prepares, makes ready, his wings for flight.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Penmark: On the west coast of Brittany, between Brest and L’Orient.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Cairrud: “The red city;” it is not known where it was situated.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Warished: cured; French, “guerir,” to heal, or recover from sickness.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Annoyeth: works mischief; from Latin, “nocco,” I hurt.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Virelays: ballads; the “virelai” was an ancient French poem of two rhymes.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Lucina the sheen: Diana the bright.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: In a Latin poem, very popular in Chaucer’s time, Pamphilus relates his amour with Galatea, setting out with the idea adopted by our poet in the lines that follow.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Sursanure: A wound healed on the surface, but festering beneath.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Orleans: Where there was a celebrated and very famous university, afterwards eclipsed by that of Paris.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Every halk and every hern: Every nook and corner, AngloSaxon, “healc,” a nook; “hyrn,” a corner.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: The word is probably derived — in “treget,” deceit or imposture — from the French “trebuchet,” a military machine; since it is evident that much and elaborate machinery must have been employed to produce the effects afterwards described.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Lissed of: eased of; released from; another form of “less” or “lessen.”

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Gironde: The river, formed by the union of the Dordogne and Garonne, on which Bourdeaux stands.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Nor gladly for that sum he would not gon: And even for that sum he would not willingly go to work.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: “Noel,” the French for Christmas — derived from “natalis,” and signifying that on that day Christ was born — came to be used as a festive cry by the people on solemn occasions.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Tables Toletanes: Toledan tables; the astronomical tables composed by order Of Alphonso II, King of Castile, about 1250 and so called because they were adapted to the city of Toledo.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: “Alnath,” Says Mr Wright, was “the first star in the horns of Aries, whence the first mansion of the moon is named.”

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Another and better reading is “a week or two.”

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: These stories are all taken from the book of St Jerome “Contra Jovinianum,” from which the Wife of Bath drew so many of her ancient instances.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Abradatas, King of Susa, was an ally of the Assyrians against Cyrus; and his wife was taken at the conquest of the Assyrian camp.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Protesilaus was the husband of Laedamia.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: The daughter of Cato of Utica, Porcia married Marcus Brutus, the friend and the assassin of Julius Caesar; when her husband died by his own hand after the battle of Philippi, she committed suicide, it is said, by swallowing live coals — all other means having been removed by her friends.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Artemisia, Queen of Caria, who built to her husband Mausolus, the splendid monument which was accounted among the wonders of the world; and who mingled her husband’s ashes with her daily drink.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Teuta: Queen of Illyria, who, after her husband’s death, made war on and was conquered by the Romans, B.C 228.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: At this point, in some manuscripts, occur thefollowing two lines: — “The same thing I say of Bilia, Of Rhodegone and of Valeria.”

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: To “boun” or “bown” is a good old word, whence comes our word “bound,” in the sense of “on the way.”

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: That from his lust yet were him lever abide: He would rather do without his pleasure.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Such apparence: such an ocular deception, or apparition more properly, disappearance — as the removal of the rocks.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: The same question is stated a the end of Boccaccio’s version of the story in the “Philocopo,” where the queen determines in favour of Aviragus.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The authenticity of the prologue is questionable.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Faconde: utterance, speech; from Latin, “facundia,” eloquence.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Slothe: other readings are “thought” and “youth.”

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Meschance: wickedness; French, “mechancete.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: This line seems to be a kind of aside thrown in by Chaucer himself.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: The various readings of this word are “churl,” or “cherl,” in the best manuscripts; “client” in the common editions, and “clerk” supported by two important manuscripts.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: 37, 38. “And she said unto her father, Let . . . me alone two months, that I may go up and down upon the mountains, and bewail my virginity, I and my fellows.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Beguiled: “cast into gaol,” according to Urry’s explanation; though we should probably understand that, if Claudius had not been sent out of the country, his death would have been secretly contrived through private detestation.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The nails and blood of Christ, by which it was then a fashion to swear.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Mediaeval medical writers; see note 36 to the Prologue to the Tales.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Boist: box; French “boite,” old form “boiste.”

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Erme: grieve; from Anglo-Saxon, “earme,” wretched.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Cardiacle: heartache; from Greek, “kardialgia.”

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Corpus Domini: God’s body.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: As to “moist,” see note 39 to the Prologue to the Tales.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: The pardoner is drunk, which explains his boastful and revealing confession of his deceits.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The outline of this Tale is to be found in the “Cento Novelle Antiche,” but the original is now lost.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Hautein: loud, lofty; from French, “hautain.”

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Radix malorum est cupiditas: “the love of money is the root of all evil” (1 Tim.vi.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Blackburied: The meaning of this is not very clear, but it is probably a periphrastic and picturesque way of indicating damnation.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Grisly: dreadful; fitted to “agrise” or horrify the listener.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Mr Wright says: “The common oaths in the Middle Ages were by the different parts of God’s body; and the popular preachers represented that profane swearers tore Christ’s body by their imprecations.”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Tombesteres: female dancers or tumblers; from AngloSaxon, “tumban,” to dance.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: “Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: The reference is probably to the diligent inquiries Herod made at the time of Christ’s birth.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: “Perhaps,” says Tyrwhitt, “Chaucer refers to Epist.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: St Jerome, in his book against Jovinian, says that so long as Adam fasted, he was in Paradise; he ate, and he was thrust out.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: “Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats; but God shall destroy both it and them.”

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: “For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ: Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Cod: bag; Anglo-Saxon, “codde;” hence peas-cod, pin-cod (pin-cushion), &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Compare with the lines which follow, the picture of the drunken messenger in the Man of Law’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Lepe: A town near Cadiz, whence a stronger wine than the Gascon vintages afforded was imported to England.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Another reading is “Fleet Street.”

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Attila was suffocated in the night by a haemorrhage, brought on by a debauch, when he was preparing a new invasion of Italy, in 453.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: “It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, nor for princes strong drink; lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted.”

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Most manuscripts, evidently in error, have “Stilbon” and “Calidone” for Chilon and Lacedaemon.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: “Swear not at all;” Christ’s words in Matt. v. 34.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: “And thou shalt swear, the lord liveth in truth, in judgement, and in righteousness.”

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: The nails that fastened Christ on the cross, which were regarded with superstitious reverence.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Hailes: An abbey in Gloucestershire, where, under the designation of “the blood of Hailes,” a portion of Christ’s blood was preserved.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Go bet: a hunting phrase; apparently its force is, “go beat up the game.”

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Haw; farm-yard, hedge Compare the French, “haie.”

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Avicen, or Avicenna, was among the distinguished physicians of the Arabian school in the eleventh century, and very popular in the Middle Ages.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Assoil: absolve. compare the Scotch law-term “assoilzie,” to acquit.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Saint Helen, according to Sir John Mandeville, found the cross of Christ deep below ground, under a rock, where the Jews had hidden it; and she tested the genuineness of the sacred tree, by raising to life a dead man laid upon it.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Prologue here given was transferred by Tyrwhitt from the place, preceding the Squire’s Tale, which it had formerly occupied; the Shipman’s Tale having no Prologue in the best manuscripts.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Lollard: A contemptuous name for the followers of Wyckliffe; presumably derived from the Latin, “lolium,” tares, as if they were the tares among the Lord’s wheat; so, a few lines below, the Shipman intimates his fear lest the Parson should “spring cockle in our clean corn.”

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Cockle: A weed, the “Agrostemma githago” of Linnaeus; perhaps named from the Anglo-Saxon, “ceocan,” because it chokes the corn.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: In this Tale Chaucer seems to have followed an old French story, which also formed the groundwork of the first story in the eighth day of the “Decameron.”

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: “He must us clothe”: So in all the manuscripts and from this and the following lines, it must be inferred that Chaucer had intended to put the Tale in the mouth of a female speaker.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Dan: a title bestowed on priests and scholars; from “Dominus,” like the Spanish “Don”.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Bruges was in Chaucer’s time the great emporium of European commerce.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: The monk had been appointed by his abbot to inspect and manage the rural property of the monastery.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Malvesie or Malmesy wine derived its name from Malvasia, a region of the Morea near Cape Malea, where it was made, as it also was on Chios and some other Greek islands.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Contour-house: counting-house; French, “comptoir.”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Under the yarde: under the rod; in pupillage; a phrase properly used of children, but employed by the Clerk in the prologue to his tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Genelon, Ganelon, or Ganilion; one of Charlemagne’s officers, whose treachery was the cause of the disastrous defeat of the Christians by the Saracens at Roncevalles; he was torn to pieces by four horses.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Elenge: From French, “eloigner,” to remove; it may mean either the lonely, cheerless condition of the priest, or the strange behaviour of the merchant in leaving him to himself.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Make a chevisance: raise money by means of a borrowing agreement; from French, “achever,” to finish; the general meaning of the word is a bargain, an agreement.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: A thousand last quad year: ever so much evil.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
