scenes.reentry: Tales of the murder of children by Jews were frequent in the Middle Ages, being probably designed to keep up the bitter feeling of the Christians against the Jews.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: 1, “Domine, dominus noster,quam admirabile est nomen tuum in universa terra.”

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: “Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings hast Thou ordained strength.” — Psalms viii.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: The ghost that in thee light: the spirit that on thee alighted; the Holy Ghost through whose power Christ was conceived.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Jewery: A quarter which the Jews were permitted to inhabit; the Old Jewry in London got its name in this way.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: St. Nicholas, even in his swaddling clothes — so says the “Breviarium Romanum” —gave promise of extraordinary virtue and holiness; for, though he sucked freely on other days, on Wednesdays and Fridays he applied to the breast only once, and that not until the evening.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: “O Alma Redemptoris Mater,” (“O soul mother of the Redeemer”) — the beginning of a hymn to the Virgin.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Antiphonere: A book of anthems, or psalms, chanted in the choir by alternate verses.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Souded; confirmed; from French, “soulde;” Latin, “solidatus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: “And they sung as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four beasts, and the elders: and no man could learn that song but the hundred and forty and four thousand, which were redeemed from the earth.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Freined: asked, inquired; from Anglo-Saxon, “frinan,” “fraegnian.”

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Halse: embrace or salute; implore: from Anglo-Saxon “hals,” the neck.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: This prologue is interesting, for the picture which it gives of Chaucer himself; riding apart from and indifferent to the rest of the pilgrims, with eyes fixed on the ground, and an “elvish”, morose, or rather self-absorbed air; portly, if not actually stout, in body; and evidently a man out of the common, as the closing words of the Host imply.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Listen, lordings, in good intent, And I will tell you verrament* *truly Of mirth and of solas,* *delight, solace All of a knight was fair and gent,* *gentle In battle and in tournament, His name was Sir Thopas.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: “The Rhyme of Sir Thopas,” as it is generally called, is introduced by Chaucer as a satire on the dull, pompous, and prolix metrical romances then in vogue.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Poppering, or Poppeling, a parish in the marches of Calais of which the famous antiquary Leland was once Rector.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: TN: The lord of Popering was the abbot of the local monastery - who could, of course, have no legitimate children.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Paindemain: Either “pain de matin,” morning bread, or “pain de Maine,” because it was made best in that province; a kind of fine white bread.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Cordewane: Cordovan; fine Spanish leather, so called from the name of the city where it was prepared

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Ciclatoun: A rich Oriental stuff of silk and gold, of which was made the circular robe of state called a “ciclaton,” from the Latin, “cyclas.”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Jane: a Genoese coin, of small value; in our old statutes called “gallihalpens,” or galley half-pence.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: TN: In Mediaeval falconry the goshawk was not regarded as a fit bird for a knight.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: A ram was the usual prize of wrestling contests.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Launcegay: spear; “azagay” is the name of a Moorish weapon, and the identity of termination is singular.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Clove-gilofre: clove-gilliflower; “Caryophyllus hortensis.”

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: TN: The sparrowhawk and parrot can only squawk unpleasantly.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: TN: The sudden and pointless changes in the stanza form are of course part of Chaucer’s parody.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Sir Oliphaunt: literally, “Sir Elephant;” Sir John Mandeville calls those animals “Olyfauntes.”

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Termagaunt: A pagan or Saracen deity, otherwise named Tervagan, and often mentioned in Middle Age literature.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: TN: His “fair bearing” would not have been much defence against a sling-stone.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: TN: “Sides small”: a conventional description for a woman, not a man.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Romances that be royal: so called because they related to Charlemagne and his family.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: TN: A knight would be expected to have a gold or silver drinking vessel.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: TN: The coat-armour or coat of arms should have had his heraldic emblems on it, not been pure white

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Charboucle: Carbuncle; French, “escarboucle;” a heraldic device resembling a jewel.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Cuirbouly: “Cuir boulli,” French, boiled or prepared leather; also used to cover shields, &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Rewel bone: No satisfactory explanation has been furnished of this word, used to describe some material from which rich saddles were made.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Spell: Tale, discourse, from Anglo-Saxon, “spellian,” to declare, tell a story.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Sir Bevis of Hampton, and Sir Guy of Warwick, two knights of great renown.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Libeux: One of Arthur’s knights, called “Ly beau desconus,” “the fair unknown.”

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: TN: The crest was a small emblem worn on top of a knight’s helmet.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Wanger: pillow; from Anglo-Saxon, “wangere,” because the “wanges;” or cheeks, rested on it.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Destrer: “destrier,” French, a war-horse; in Latin, “dextrarius,” as if led by the right hand.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Sir Percival de Galois, whose adventures were written in more than 60,000 verses by Chretien de Troyes, one of the oldest and best French romancers, in 1191.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Chaucer crowns the satire on the romanticists by making the very landlord of the Tabard cry out in indignant disgust against the stuff which he had heard recited — the good Host ascribing to sheer ignorance the string of pompous platitudes and prosaic details which Chaucer had uttered.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Drafty: worthless, vile; no better than draff or dregs; from the Anglo-Saxon, “drifan” to drive away, expel.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Tale of Melibœus is literally translated from a French story, or rather “treatise,” in prose, entitled “Le Livre de Melibee et de Dame Prudence,” of which two manuscripts, both dating from the fifteenth century, are preserved in the British Museum.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: The lines which follow are a close translation of the original Latin, which reads: “Quis matrem, nisi mentis inops, in funere nati Flere vetet? non hoc illa monenda loco.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: See the conversation between Pluto and Proserpine, in the Merchant’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: “Thy name,” she says, “is Melibœus; that is to say, a man that drinketh honey.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Los: reputation; from the past participle of the Anglo-Saxon, “hlisan” to celebrate.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Corpus Madrian: the body of St. Maternus, of Treves.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: That her misdoth or saith: that does or says any thing to offend her.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Cope: An ecclesiastcal vestment covering all the body like a cloak.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Though he were shorn full high upon his pan: though he were tonsured, as the clergy are.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Imps: shoots, branches; from Anglo-Saxon, “impian,” German, “impfen,” to implant, ingraft.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Lusheburghes: base or counterfeit coins; so called because struck at Luxemburg.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Monk’s Tale is founded in its main features on Bocccacio’s work, “De Casibus Virorum Illustrium;” (“Stories of Illustrious Men”) but Chaucer has taken the separate stories of which it is composed from different authors, and dealt with them after his own fashion.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Boccaccio opens his book with Adam, whose story is told at much greater length than here.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Boccaccio also tells the story of Samson; but Chaucer seems, by his quotation a few lines below, to have taken his version direct from the sacred book.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Oliveres: olive trees; French, “oliviers.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “Liber Judicum,” the Book of Judges; chap. xv.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Querne: mill; from Anglo-Saxon, “cyrran,” to turn, “cweorn,” a mill, 7.Harpies: the Stymphalian Birds, which fed on human flesh.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Busiris, king of Egypt, was wont to sacrifice all foreigners coming to his dominions.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: The feats of Hercules here recorded are not all these known as the “twelve labours;” for instance, the cleansing of the Augean stables, and the capture of Hippolyte’s girdle are not in this list — other and less famous deeds of the hero taking their place.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Trophee: One of the manuscripts has a marginal reference to “Tropheus vates Chaldaeorum” (“Tropheus the prophet of the Chaldees”); but it is not known what author Chaucer meant — unless the reference is to a passage in the “Filostrato” of Boccaccio, on which Chaucer founded his “Troilus and Cressida,” and which Lydgate mentions, under the name of “Trophe,” as having been translated by Chaucer.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Pres: near; French, “pres;” the meaning seems to be, this nearer, lower world.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Odenatus, who, for his services to the Romans, received from Gallienus the title of “Augustus;” he was assassinated in A.D.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Sapor was king of Persia, who made the Emperor Valerian prisoner, conquered Syria, and was pressing triumphantly westward when he was met and defeated by Odenatus and Zenobia.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Aurelain became Emperor in A.D.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Vitremite: The signification of this word, which is spelled in several ways, is not known.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Great part of this “tragedy” of Nero is really borrowed, however, from the “Romance of the Rose.”

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Trice: thrust; from Anglo-Saxon, “thriccan.”

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: So, in the Man of Law’s Tale, the Sultaness promises her son that she will “reny her lay.”

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: As the “tragedy” of Holofernes is founded on the book of Judith, so is that of Antiochus on the Second Book of the Maccabees, chap. ix.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: By the insurgents under the leadership of Judas Maccabeus; 2 Macc. chap. viii.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Six: the highest cast on a dicing-cube; here representing the highest favour of fortune.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Pompey had married his daughter Julia to Caesar; but she died six years before Pompey’s final overthrow.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: At the battle of Pharsalia, B.C.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Word and end: apparently a corruption of the Anglo-Saxon phrase, “ord and end,” meaning the whole, the beginning and the end.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: At the opening of the story of Croesus, Chaucer has copied from his own translation of Boethius; but the story is mainly taken from the “Romance of the Rose”

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: “This reflection,” says Tyrwhttt, “seems to have been suggested by one which follows soon after the mention of Croesus in the passage just cited from Boethius.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Pedro the Cruel, King of Aragon, against whom his brother Henry rebelled.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Not the Oliver of Charlemagne — but a traitorous Oliver of Armorica, corrupted by a bribe.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Pierre de Lusignan, King of Cyprus, who captured Alexandria in 1363 (see note 6 to the Prologue to the Tales).

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Bernabo Visconti, Duke of Milan, was deposed and imprisoned by his nephew, and died a captive in 1385.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: The story of Ugolino is told in the 33rd Canto of the “Inferno.”

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The request is justified by the description of Monk in the Prologue as “an out-rider, that loved venery.”

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: On this Tyrwhitt remarks; “I know not how it has happened, that in the principal modern languages, John, or its equivalent, is a name of contempt or at least of slight.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Compare French, “entamer”, to cut the first piece off a joint; thence to begin.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Tale of the Nun’s Priest is founded on the fifth chapter of an old French metrical “Romance of Renard;” the same story forming one of the fables of Marie, the translator of the Breton Lays.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Tyrwhitt quotes two statutes of Edward III, in which “deys” are included among the servants employed in agricultural pursuits; the name seems to have originally meant a servant who gave his labour by the day, but afterwards to have been appropriated exclusively to one who superintended or worked in a dairy.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Orgon: here licentiously used for the plural, “organs” or “orgons,” corresponding to the plural verb “gon” in the next line.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Horloge: French, “clock.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Embattell’d: indented on the upper edge like the battlements of a castle.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: My lefe is fare in land: This seems to have been the refrain of some old song, and its precise meaning is uncertain.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: “Avoi!” is the word here rendered “away!”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: “Ne do no force of dreams:” “Somnia ne cares;” — Cato “De Moribus,” 1 ii, dist.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Centaury: the herb so called because by its virtue the centaur Chiron was healed when the poisoned arrow of Hercules had accidentally wounded his foot.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Fumetere: the herb “fumitory.”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Catapuce: spurge; a plant of purgative qualities.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Gaitre-berries: dog-wood berries.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: One of the greatest authors that men read: Cicero, who in his book “De Divinatione” tells this and the following story, though in contrary order and with many differences.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Haled or hylled; from Anglo-Saxon “helan” hid, concealed

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Kenelm succeeded his father as king of the Saxon realm of Mercia in 811, at the age of seven years; but he was slain by his ambitious aunt Quendrada.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Mercenrike: the kingdom of Mercia; Anglo-Saxon, Myrcnarice.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Cicero (“De Republica,” lib. vi.) wrote the Dream of Scipio, in which the Younger relates the appearance of the Elder Africanus, and the counsels and exhortations which the shade addressed to the sleeper.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: See the Monk’s Tale for this story.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Andromache’s dream will not be found in Homer; It is related in the book of the fictitious Dares Phrygius, the most popular authority during the Middle Ages for the history of the Trojan War.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: In principio: In the beginning; the first words of Genesis and of the Gospel of John.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Mulier est hominis confusio: This line is taken from the same fabulous conference between the Emperor Adrian and the philosopher Secundus, whence Chaucer derived some of the arguments in praise of poverty employed in the Wife of Bath’s Tale proper.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Col-fox: a blackish fox, so called because of its likeness to coal, according to Skinner; though more probably the prefix has a reproachful meaning, and is in some way connected with the word “cold” as, some forty lines below, it is applied to the prejudicial counsel of women, and as frequently it is used to describe “sighs” and other tokens of grief, and “cares” or “anxieties.”

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Undern: In this case, the meaning of “evening” or “afternoon” can hardly be applied to the word, which must be taken to signify some early hour of the forenoon.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: See note 9 to the Shipman’s Tale and note 28 to the Monk’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Greek Sinon: The inventor of the Trojan Horse.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Boult it from the bren: Examine the matter thoroughly; a metaphor taken from the sifting of meal, to divide the fine flour from the bran.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Thomas Bradwardine, Archbishop of Canterbury in the thirteenth century, who wrote a book, “De Causa Dei,” in controversy with Pelagius; and also numerous other treatises, among them some on predestination.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: In a popular mediaveal Latin treatise by one Theobaldus, entitled “Physiologus de Naturis XII.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: “Nigellus Wireker,” says Urry’s Glossary, “a monk and precentor of Canterbury, wrote a Latin poem intituled ‘Speculum Speculorum,’ (‘The mirror of mirrors’) dedicated to William Longchamp, Bishop of Ely, and Lord Chancellor; wherein, under the fable of an Ass (which he calls ‘Burnellus’) that desired a longer tail, is represented the folly of such as are not content with their own condition.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Flattour: flatterer; French, “flatteur.”

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Losengeour: deceiver, cozener; the word had analogues in the French “losengier,” and the Spanish “lisongero.”

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: Dan Russel: Master Russet; a name given to the fox, from his reddish colour.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Geoffrey de Vinsauf was the author of a well-known mediaeval treatise on composition in various poetical styles of which he gave examples.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: “Priamum altaria ad ipsa trementem Traxit, et in multo lapsantem sanguine nati Implicuitque comam laeva, dextraque coruscum Extulit, ac lateri capulo tenus abdidit ensem.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: Jack Straw: The leader of a Kentish rising, in the reign of Richard II, in 1381, by which the Flemish merchants in London were great sufferers.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: Beams: trumpets; Anglo-Saxon, “bema.”

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.” — 2 Tim. iii.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: “Sir Nunne’s Priest,” our hoste said anon, “Y-blessed be thy breech, and every stone; This was a merry tale of Chanticleer.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The sixteen lines appended to the Tale of the Nun’s Priest seem, as Tyrwhitt observes, to commence the prologue to the succeeding Tale — but the difficulty is to determine which that Tale should be.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: This Tale was originally composed by Chaucer as a separate work, and as such it is mentioned in the “Legend of Good Women” under the title of “The Life of Saint Cecile”.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Leas: leash, snare; the same as “las,” oftener used by Chaucer.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: The nativity and assumption of the Virgin Mary formed the themes of some of St Bernard’s most eloquent sermons.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Compare with this stanza the fourth stanza of the Prioress’s Tale, the substance of which is the same.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “But he answered and said, it is not meet to take the children’s bread, and cast it to dogs.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: These are Latin puns: Heaven’s lily - “Coeli lilium”; The way of blind - “Caeci via”; Heaven and Lia - from “Coeli”, heaven, and “Ligo,” to bind; Heaven and Leos - from Coeli and “Laos,” (Ionian Greek) or “Leos” (Attic Greek), the people.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: This passage suggests Horace’s description of the wise man, who, among other things, is “in se ipse totus, teres, atque rotundus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Louting: lingering, or lying concealed; the Latin original has “Inter sepulchra martyrum latiantem” (“hiding among the tombs of martyrs”)

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: The fourteen lines within brackets are supposed to have been originally an interpolation in the Latin legend, from which they are literally translated.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Engine: wit; the devising or constructive faculty; Latin, “ingenium.”

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Cold: wretched, distressful; see note 22 to the Nun’s Priest’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Corniculere: The secretary or registrar who was charged with publishing the acts, decrees and orders of the prefect.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” — 2 Tim. iv.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Did him to-beat: Caused him to be cruelly or fatally beaten; the force of the “to” is intensive.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: “The introduction,” says Tyrwhitt, “of the Canon’s Yeoman to tell a Tale at a time when so many of the original characters remain to be called upon, appears a little extraordinary.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Fully five mile: From some place which the loss of the Second Nun’s Prologue does not enable us to identify.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Peytrel: the breast-plate of a horse’s harness; French, “poitrail.”

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: A maile twyfold: a double valise; a wallet hanging across the crupper on either side of the horse.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Multiply: transmute metals, in the attempt to multiply gold and silver by alchemy.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: “Conscius ipse sibi de se putat omnia dici” (“The conspirator believes that everything spoken refers to himself”) — “De Moribus,” I. i. dist.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: With this Canon I dwelt have seven year, And of his science am I ne’er the near* *nearer All that I had I have lost thereby, And, God wot, so have many more than I. Where I was wont to be right fresh and gay Of clothing, and of other good array Now may I wear an hose upon mine head; And where my colour was both fresh and red, Now is it wan, and of a leaden hue (Whoso it useth, sore shall he it rue); And of my swink* yet bleared is mine eye; *labour Lo what advantage is to multiply!

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Tale of the Canon’s Yeoman, like those of the Wife of Bath and the Pardoner, is made up of two parts; a long general introduction, and the story proper.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: In Froissart’s French, “a jeu partie” is used to signify a game or contest in which the chances were exactly equal for both sides.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Squames: Scales; Latin, “squamae.”

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Descensories: vessels for distillation “per descensum;” they were placed under the fire, and the spirit to be extracted was thrown downwards.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Seared pokettes: the meaning of this phrase is obscure; but if we take the reading “cered poketts,” from the Harleian manuscript, we are led to the supposition that it signifies receptacles — bags or pokes — prepared with wax for some process.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Argoil: potter’s clay, used for luting or closing vessels in the laboratories of the alchemists; Latin, “argilla;” French, “argile.”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Citrination: turning to a citrine colour, or yellow, by chemical action; that was the colour which proved the philosopher’s stone.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Ingots: not, as in its modern meaning, the masses of metal shaped by pouring into moulds; but the moulds themslves into which the fused metal was poured.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Threpe: name; from Anglo-Saxon, “threapian.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Bratt: coarse cloak; Anglo-Saxon, “bratt.”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Long on: in consequence of; the modern vulgar phrase “all along of,” or “all along on,” best conveys the force of the words in the text.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Annualere: a priest employed in singing “annuals” or anniversary masses for the dead, without any cure of souls; the office was such as, in the Prologue to the Tales, Chaucer praises the Parson for not seeking: Nor “ran unto London, unto Saint Poul’s, to seeke him a chantery for souls.”

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Mortify: a chemical phrase, signifying the dissolution of quicksilver in acid.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Blin: cease; from Anglo-Saxon, “blinnan,” to desist.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Name: took; from Anglo-Saxon, “niman,” to take.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: See note 5 to Chaucer’s tale of Melibœus.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Grame: sorrow; Anglo-Saxon, “gram;” German, “Gram.”

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Arnaldus Villanovanus, or Arnold de Villeneuve, was a distinguished French chemist and physician of the fourteenth century; his “Rosarium Philosophorum” was a favourite text-book with the alchemists of the generations that succeeded.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Hermes Trismegistus, counsellor of Osiris, King of Egypt, was credited with the invention of writing and hieroglyphics, the drawing up of the laws of the Egyptians, and the origination of many sciences and arts.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Secret of secrets: “Secreta Secretorum;” a treatise, very popular in the Middle Ages, supposed to contain the sum of Aristotle’s instructions to Alexander.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Hamuelis tabula chymica” (“The chemical tables of Senior Zadith, son of Hamuel”); and the story here told of Plato and his disciple was there related of Solomon, but with some variations.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Ignotum per ignotius: To explain the unknown by the more unknown.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Though he multiply term of his live: Though he pursue the alchemist’s art all his days.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Bob-up-and-down: Mr Wright supposes this to be the village of Harbledown, near Canterbury, which is situated on a hill, and near which there are many ups and downs in the road.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Dun is in the mire: a proverbial saying.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: The mention of the Cook here, with no hint that he had already told a story, confirms the indication given by the imperfect condition of his Tale, that Chaucer intended to suppress the Tale altogether, and make him tell a story in some other place.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: The quintain; called “fan” or “vane,” because it turned round like a weather-cock.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Referring to the classification of wine, according to its effects on a man, given in the old “Calendrier des Bergiers,” The man of choleric temperament has “wine of lion;” the sanguine, “wine of ape;” the phlegmatic, “wine of sheep;” the melancholic, “wine of sow.”

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: The pose: a defluxion or rheum which stops the nose and obstructs the voice.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Bring thee to his lure: A phrase in hawking — to recall a hawk to the fist; the meaning here is, that the Cook may one day bring the Manciple to account, or pay him off, for the rebuke of his drunkenness.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: “The fable of ‘The Crow,’ says Tyrwhitt, “which is the subject of the Manciple’s Tale, has been related by so many authors, from Ovid down to Gower, that it is impossible to say whom Chaucer principally followed.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: See the parallel to this passage in the Squire’s Tale, and note 34 to that tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Wantrust: distrust — want of trust; so “wanhope,” despair - - want of hope.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: This is quoted in the French “Romance of the Rose,” from Cato “De Moribus,” 1. i., dist.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “Semel emissum volat irrevocabile verbum.”

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: This caution is also from Cato “De Moribus,” 1. i., dist.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Rom, ram, ruf: a contemptuous reference to the alliterative poetry which was at that time very popular, in preference even, it would seem, to rhyme, in the northern parts of the country, where the language was much more barbarous and unpolished than in the south.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Perfect glorious pilgrimage: the word is used here to signify the shrine, or destination, to which pilgrimage is made.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Parson’s Tale is believed to be a translation, more or less free, from some treatise on penitence that was in favour about Chaucer’s time.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: See Note 3 to the Sompnour’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Just before, the Parson had cited the words of Job to God (Job x.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “I have lost everything - my time and my work.”

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Accidie: neglectfulness or indifference; from the Greek, akedeia.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: The pax: an image which was presented to the people to be kissed, at that part of the mass where the priest said, “Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum.”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Three ways of ornamenting clothes with lace, &c.; in barring it was laid on crossways, in ounding it was waved, in paling it was laid on lengthways.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Penitencer: a priest who enjoined penance in extraordinary cases.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: To be houseled: to receive the holy sacrament; from AngloSaxon, “husel;” Latin, “hostia,” or “hostiola,” the host.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: It was a frequent penance among the chivalric orders to wear mail shirts next the skin.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Surquedrie: presumption; from old French, “surcuider,” to think arrogantly, be full of conceit.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The genuineness and real significance of this “Prayer of Chaucer,” usually called his “Retractation,” have been warmly disputed.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: “[You] Who with the Father and the Holy Spirit livest and reignest God for ever and ever.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: So the Man of Law, in the prologue to his Tale, is made to say that Chaucer “can but lewedly (ignorantly or imperfectly) on metres and on rhyming craftily.”

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Born: burnish, polish: the poet means, that his verses do not display the eloquence or brilliancy of Cicero in setting forth his subject-matter.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Galfrid: Geoffrey de Vinsauf to whose treatise on poetical composition a less flattering allusion is made in The Nun’s Priest’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: Stirp: race, stock; Latin, “stirps.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Calliope is the epic muse — “sister” to the other eight.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Melpomene was the tragic muse.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: The same is said of Griselda, in The Clerk’s Tale; though she was of tender years, “yet in the breast of her virginity there was inclos’d a sad and ripe corage”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: The confusion which Chaucer makes between Cithaeron and Cythera, has already been remarked.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Balais: Bastard rubies; said to be so called from Balassa, the Asian country where they were found.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Spenser, in his description of the House of Busirane, speaks of the sad distress into which Phoebus was plunged by Cupid, in revenge for the betrayal of “his mother’s wantonness, when she with Mars was meint [mingled] in joyfulness”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, was won to wife by Admetus, King of Pherae, who complied with her father’s demand that he should come to claim her in a chariot drawn by lions and boars.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: In the prologue to the “Legend of Good Women,” Chaucer says that behind the God of Love, upon the green, he “saw coming in ladies nineteen;” but the stories of only nine good women are there told.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Arras: tapestry of silk, made at Arras, in France.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Danger, in the Provencal Courts of Love, was the allegorical personification of the husband; and Disdain suitably represents the lover’s corresponding difficulty from the side of the lady.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: In The Knight’s Tale, Emily’s yellow hair is braided in a tress, or plait, that hung a yard long behind her back; so that, both as regards colour and fashion, a singular resemblance seems to have existed between the female taste of 1369 and that of 1869.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: In an old monkish story — reproduced by Boccaccio, and from him by La Fontaine in the Tale called “Les Oies de Frere Philippe” — a young man is brought up without sight or knowledge of women, and, when he sees them on a visit to the city, he is told that they are geese.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Tabernacle: A shrine or canopy of stone, supported by pillars.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: Mister folk: handicraftsmen, or tradesmen, who have learned “mysteries.”

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: The loves “Of Queen Annelida and False Arcite” formed the subject of a short unfinished poem by Chaucer, which was afterwards worked up into The Knight’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Blue was the colour of truth.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Blife: quickly, eagerly; for “blive” or “belive.”

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: It will be seen afterwards that Philogenet does not relish it, and pleads for its relaxation.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Feat: dainty, neat, handsome; the same as “fetis,” oftener used in Chaucer; the adverb “featly” is still used, as applied to dancing, &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Solomon was beguiled by his heathenish wives to forsake the worship of the true God; Samson fell a victim to the wiles of Delilah.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Compare the speech of Proserpine to Pluto, in The Merchant’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: See note 91 to the Knight’s Tale for a parallel.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Flaw: yellow; Latin, “flavus,” French, “fauve.”

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Bass: kiss; French, “baiser;” and hence the more vulgar “buss.”

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Maximian: Cornelius Maximianus Gallus flourished in the time of the Emperor Anastasius; in one of his elegies, he professed a preference for flaming and somewhat swelling lips, which, when he tasted them, would give him full kisses.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Dwale: sleeping potion, narcotic.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: Environ: around; French, “a l’environ.”

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Cast off thine heart: i.e. from confidence in her.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: Nesh: soft, delicate; Anglo-Saxon, “nese.”

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: Perfection: Perfectly holy life, in the performance of vows of poverty, chastity, obedience, and other modes of mortifying the flesh.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: All the sin must on our friendes be: who made us take the vows before they knew our own dispositions, or ability, to keep them.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: Cope: The large vestment worn in singing the service in the choir.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: The three of fatal destiny: The three Fates.

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: Cythere: Cytherea — Venus, so called from the name of the island, Cythera, into which her worship was first introduced from Phoenicia.

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: Avaunter: Boaster; Philobone calls him out.

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: The statute: i.e. the 16th.

scenes.title: Chapter 42
scenes.reentry: 768 et seqq., where a general description of Envy is given.

scenes.title: Chapter 43
scenes.reentry: Golden Love and Leaden Love represent successful and unsuccessful love; the first kindled by Cupid’s golden darts, the second by his leaden arrows.

scenes.title: Chapter 44
scenes.reentry: “Domine, labia mea aperies — et os meam annunciabit laudem tuam” (“Lord, open my lips — and my mouth will announce your praise”) Psalms li.

scenes.title: Chapter 45
scenes.reentry: “Venite, exultemus,” (“Come, let us rejoice”) are the first words of Psalm xcv. called the “Invitatory.”

scenes.title: Chapter 46
scenes.reentry: “Domine Dominus noster:” The opening words of Psalm viii.; “O Lord our Lord.”

scenes.title: Chapter 47
scenes.reentry: “Coeli enarrant:” Psalm xix.

scenes.title: Chapter 48
scenes.reentry: I; “The earth is the Lord’s and the fulness thereof.”

scenes.title: Chapter 49
scenes.reentry: “Jube, Domine:” “Command, O Lord;” from Matthew xiv.

scenes.title: Chapter 51
scenes.reentry: “Te Deum Amoris:” “Thee, God of Love (we praise).”

scenes.title: Chapter 52
scenes.reentry: Not Tubal, who was the worker in metals; but Jubal, his brother, “who was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ” (Genesis iv.

scenes.title: Chapter 53
scenes.reentry: With this began the “Laudes,” or morning service of praise.

scenes.title: Chapter 54
scenes.reentry: “Jubilate:” Psalm c.

scenes.title: Chapter 55
scenes.reentry: “Benedicite:” “Bless ye the Lord;” the opening of the Song of the Three Children

scenes.title: Chapter 56
scenes.reentry: “Laudate:” Psalm cxlvii.; “Praise ye the Lord.”

scenes.title: Chapter 57
scenes.reentry: “O admirabile:” Psalm viii 1; “O Lord our God, how excellent is thy name.”

scenes.title: Chapter 58
scenes.reentry: “Benedictus”: The first word of the Song of Zacharias (Luke i.

scenes.title: Chapter 59
scenes.reentry: In The Knight’s Tale we have exemplifications of the custom of gathering and wearing flowers and branches on May Day; where Emily, “doing observance to May,” goes into the garden at sunrise and gathers flowers, “party white and red, to make a sotel garland for her head”; and again, where Arcite rides to the fields “to make him a garland of the greves; were it of woodbine, or of hawthorn leaves” THE CUCKOO AND THE NIGHTINGALE.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: These two lines occur also in The Knight’s Tale; they commence the speech of Theseus on the love follies of Palamon and Arcite, whom the Duke has just found fighting in the forest.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: A stronger reading is “all.”

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: “Ocy, ocy,” is supposed to come from the Latin “occidere,” to kill; or rather the old French, “occire,” “occis,” denoting the doom which the nightingale imprecates or supplicates on all who do offence to Love.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: 5.”But if he be away therewith, y-wis, He may full soon of age have his hair”: Unless he be always fortunate in love pursuits, he may full soon have gray hair, through his anxieties.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: It was of evil omen to hear the cuckoo before the nightingale or any other bird.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: The Queen: Philippa of Hainault, wife of Edward III.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: “The Dream of Scipio” — “Somnium Scipionis” — occupies most of the sixth book of Cicero’s “Republic;” which, indeed, as it has come down to us, is otherwise imperfect.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Y-nome: taken; past participle of “nime,” from Anglo-Saxon, “niman,” to take.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: His grace: the favour which the gods would show him, in delivering Carthage into his hands.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: “Vestra vero, quae dicitur, vita mors est.” (“Truly, as is said, your life is a death”)

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: The nine spheres are God, or the highest heaven, constraining and containing all the others; the Earth, around which the planets and the highest heaven revolve; and the seven planets: the revolution of all producing the “music of the spheres.”

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Clear: illustrious, noble; Latin, “clarus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: The sicke mette he drinketh of the tun: The sick man dreams that he drinks wine, as one in health.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: The significance of the poet’s looking to the NNW is not plain; his window may have faced that way.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: The idea of the twin gates, leading to the Paradise and the Hell of lovers, may have been taken from the description of the gates of dreams in the Odyssey and the Aeneid; but the iteration of “Through me men go” far more directly suggests the legend on Dante’s gate of Hell:— Per me si va nella citta dolente, Per me si va nell’ eterno dolore; Per me si va tra la perduta gente.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: A powerful though homely description of torment; the sufferers being represented as fish enclosed in a weir from which all the water has been withdrawn.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Compare with this catalogue raisonne of trees the ampler list given by Spenser in “The Faerie Queen,” book i. canto i.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: If Chaucer had any special trio of courtiers in his mind when he excluded so many names, we may suppose them to be Charms, Sorcery, and Leasings who, in The Knight’s Tale, come after Bawdry and Riches — to whom Messagerie (the carrying of messages) and Meed (reward, bribe) may correspond.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: The dove was the bird sacred to Venus; hence Ovid enumerates the peacock of Juno, Jove’s armour bearing bird, “Cythereiadasque columbas” (“And the Cythereian doves”) — “Metamorphoses. xv.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Priapus: fitly endowed with a place in the Temple of Love, as being the embodiment of the principle of fertility in flocks and the fruits of the earth.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: 433), describes the confusion of Priapus when, in the night following a feast of sylvan and Bacchic deities, the braying of the ass of Silenus wakened the company to detect the god in a furtive amatory expedition.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: Hautain: haughty, lofty; French, “hautain.”

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Well to my pay: Well to my satisfaction; from French, “payer,” to pay, satisfy; the same word often occurs, in the phrases “well apaid,” and “evil apaid.”

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Valentia, in Spain, was famed for the fabrication of fine and transparent stuffs.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: The obvious reference is to the proverbial “Sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus,” (“Love is frozen without freedom and food”) quoted in Terence, “Eunuchus,” act iv. scene v.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Cypride: Venus; called “Cypria,” or “Cypris,” from the island of Cyprus, in which her worship was especially celebrated.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, was seduced by Jupiter, turned into a bear by Diana, and placed afterwards, with her son, as the Great Bear among the stars.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Prest: ready; French, “pret.”

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Alanus de Insulis, a Sicilian poet and orator of the twelfth century, who wrote a book “De Planctu Naturae” — “The Complaint of Nature.”

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: The falcon was borne on the hand by the highest personages, not merely in actual sport, but to be caressed and petted, even on occasions of ceremony, Hence also it is called the “gentle” falcon — as if its high birth and breeding gave it a right to august society.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: The merlion: elsewhere in the same poem called “emerlon;” French, “emerillon;” the merlin, a small hawk carried by ladies.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: The scorning jay: scorning humbler birds, out of pride of his fine plumage.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: The false lapwing: full of stratagems and pretences to divert approaching danger from the nest where her young ones are.

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: The sparrow, Venus’ son: Because sacred to Venus.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: Coming with the spring, the nightingale is charmingly said to call forth the new leaves.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Many-coloured wings, like those of peacocks, were often given to angels in paintings of the Middle Ages; and in accordance with this fashion Spenser represents the Angel that guarded Sir Guyon (“Faerie Queen,” book ii. canto vii.) as having wings “decked with diverse plumes, like painted jay’s.”

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: The pheasant, scorner of the cock by night: The meaning of this passage is not very plain; it has been supposed, however, to refer to the frequent breeding of pheasants at night with domestic poultry in the farmyard — thus scorning the sway of the cock, its rightful monarch.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: The waker goose: Chaucer evidently alludes to the passage in Ovid describing the crow of Apollo, which rivalled the spotless doves, “Nec servataris vigili Capitolia voce cederet anseribus” — “nor would it yield (in whiteness) to the geese destined with wakeful or vigilant voice to save the Capitol” (“Metam.,” ii.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: The cuckoo ever unkind: the significance of this epithet is amply explained by the poem of “The Cuckoo and the Nightingale.”

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: The drake, destroyer: of the ducklings — which, if not prevented, he will kill wholesale.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: The stork is conspicuous for faithfulness to all family obligations, devotion to its young, and care of its parent birds in their old age.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: The cormorant feeds upon fish, so voraciously, that when the stomach is crammed it will often have the gullet and bill likewise full, awaiting the digestion of the rest.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: So called from the evil omens supposed to be afforded by their harsh cries.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: The fieldfare visits this country only in hard wintry weather.

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: “Formel,” strictly or originally applied to the female of the eagle and hawk, is here used generally of the female of all birds; “tercel” is the corresponding word applied to the male.

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: Entriketh: entangles, ensnares; french, “intriguer,” to perplex; hence “intricate.”

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: Entremette him of: meddle with; French, “entremettre,” to interfere.

scenes.title: Chapter 42
scenes.reentry: The duck exhorts the contending lovers to be of light heart and sing, for abundance of other ladies were at their command.

scenes.title: Chapter 43
scenes.reentry: Solain: single, alone; the same word originally as “sullen.”

scenes.title: Chapter 44
scenes.reentry: The cuckoo is distinguished by its habit of laying its eggs in the nests of other and smaller birds, such as the hedge-sparrow (“heggsugg”); and its young, when hatched, throw the eggs or nestlings of the true parent bird out of the nest, thus engrossing the mother’s entire care.

scenes.title: Chapter 45
scenes.reentry: “Who well loves, late forgets;” the refrain of the roundel inculcates the duty of constancy, which has been imposed on the three tercels by the decision of the Court.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The Bull: the sign of Taurus, which the sun enters in May.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: The young oak leaves are red or ashen coloured.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Chaucer here again refers to the superstition, noticed in “The Cuckoo and the Nightingale,” that it was of good omen to hear the nightingale before the cuckoo upon the advent of both with spring.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: The arbour was furnished with seats, which had been newly covered with turf.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “Yede” or “yead,” is the old form of go.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Sote: fool — French “sot.”

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: See note 59 to The Court of Love

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Agnus castus: the chaste-tree; a kind of willow.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Roundell: French, “rondeau;” a song that comes round again to the verse with which it opened, or that is taken up in turn by each of the singers.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: In modern French form, “Sous la feuille, devers moi, son et mon joli coeur est endormi” — “Under the foliage, towards me, his and my jolly heart is gone to sleep.”

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: Prester John: The half-mythical Eastern potentate, who is now supposed to have been, not a Christian monarch of Abyssinia, but the head of the Indian empire before Zenghis Khan’s conquest.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Oak cerrial: of the species of oak which Pliny, in his “Natural History,” calls “cerrus.”

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Tartarium: Cloth of Tars, or of Tortona.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Bargaret: bergerette, or pastoral song.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: “Si douce est la margarete.”: “So sweet is the daisy” (“la marguerite”).

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: To make their joustes: the meaning is not very obvious; but in The Knight’s Tale “jousts and array” are in some editions made part of the adornment of the Temple of Venus; and as the word “jousts” would there carry the general meaning of “preparations” to entertain or please a lover, in the present case it may have a similar force.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Gramercy: “grand merci,” French; great thanks.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: The Nine Worthies, who at our day survive in the Seven Champions of Christendom.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: The famous Knights of King Arthur, who, being all esteemed equal in valour and noble qualities, sat at a round table, so that none should seem to have precedence over the rest.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: The twelve peers of Charlemagne (les douze pairs), chief among whom were Roland and Oliver.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Chaucer speaks as if, at least for the purposes of his poetry, he believed that Edward III. did not establish a new, but only revived an old, chivalric institution, when be founded the Order of the Garter.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Laurer: laurel-tree; French, “laurier.”

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: The meaning is: “Witness the practice of Rome, that was the founder of all knighthood and marvellous deeds; and I refer for corroboration to Titus Livius” who, in several passages, has mentioned the laurel crown as the highest military honour.

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Malebouche: Slander, personified under the title of Evil-mouth — Italian, “Malbocca;” French, “Malebouche.”

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Under support of them that list it read: the phrase means — trusting to the goodwill of my reader.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: In press: into a crowd, into the press of competitors for favour; not, it need hardly be said, “into the press” in the modern sense — printing was not invented for a century after this was written.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: Rood: the cross on which Christ was crucified; Anglo-Saxon, “Rode.”

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Well worth of this thing greate clerks: Great scholars set much worth upon this thing — that is, devote much labour, attach much importance, to the subject of dreams.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: The poet briefly refers to the description of the House of Somnus, in Ovid’s “Metamorphoses,” 1. xi.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: See the account of the vision of Croesus in The Monk’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: The meaning of the allusion is not clear; but the story of the pilgrims and the peas is perhaps suggested by the line following — “to make lithe [soft] what erst was hard.”

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: Corsaint: The “corpus sanctum” — the holy body, or relics, preserved in the shrine.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: So, in the Temple of Venus described in The Knight’s Tale, the Goddess is represented as “naked floating in the large sea”.

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Vulcano: Vulcan, the husband of Venus.

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: Ered: ploughed; Latin, “arare,” Anglo-Saxon, “erean,” plough.

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: Sours: Soaring ascent; a hawk was said to be “on the soar” when he mounted, “on the sours” or “souse” when he descended on the prey, and took it in flight.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: This is only one among many instances in which Chaucer disclaims the pursuits of love; and the description of his manner of life which follows is sufficient to show that the disclaimer was no mere mock-humble affectation of a gallant.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: This reference, approximately fixing the date at which the poem was composed, points clearly to Chaucer’s daily work as Comptroller of the Customs — a post which he held from 1374 to 1386.

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: This is a frank enough admission that the poet was fond of good cheer; and the effect of his “little abstinence” on his corporeal appearance is humorously described in the Prologue to the Tale of Sir Thopas, where the Host compliments Chaucer on being as well shapen in the waist as himself.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: “To make the beard” means to befool or deceive.

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: Love-days: see note 21 to the Prologue to the Canterbury Tales.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: If this reference is to any book of Chaucer’s in which the House of Fame was mentioned, the book has not come down to us.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Saint Julian was the patron of hospitality; so the Franklin, in the Prologue to The Canterbury Tales is said to be “Saint Julian in his country,” for his open house and liberal cheer.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: The laurel-tree is sacred to Apollo.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: French, “roche,” a rock.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: St. Thomas of Kent: Thomas a Beckett, whose shrine was at Canterbury.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: The half or side of the rock which was towards the poet, was inscribed with, etc.

scenes.title: Chapter 22
scenes.reentry: Cop: summit; German, “kopf”; the head.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Gestiours: tellers of stories; reciters of brave feats or “gests.”

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: Arion: the celebrated Greek bard and citharist, who, in the seventh century before Christ, lived at the court of Periander, tyrant of Corinth.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Chiron the Centaur was renowned for skill in music and the arts, which he owed to the teaching of Apollo and Artemis.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: Glasgerion is the subject of a ballad given in “Percy’s Reliques,” where we are told that “Glasgerion was a king’s own son, And a harper he was good; He harped in the king’s chamber, Where cup and candle stood.”

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: Cornemuse: bagpipe; French, “cornemuse.”

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: Dulcet: a kind of pipe, probably corresponding with the “dulcimer;” the idea of sweet — French, “doux;” Latin, “dulcis” — is at the root of both words.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: In the early printed editions of Chaucer, the two names are “Citherus” and “Proserus;” in the manuscript which Mr Bell followed (No.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: Marsyas: The Phrygian, who, having found the flute of Athena, which played of itself most exquisite music, challenged Apollo to a contest, the victor in which was to do with the vanquished as he pleased.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: The German (Deutsche) language, in Chaucer’s time, had not undergone that marked literary division into German and Dutch which was largely accomplished through the influence of the works of Luther and the other Reformers.

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: Reyes: a kind of dance, or song to be accompanied with dancing.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Beam: horn, trumpet; Anglo-Saxon, “bema.”

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: Messenus: Misenus, son of Aeolus, the companion and trumpeter of Aeneas, was drowned near the Campanian headland called Misenum after his name.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: Joab’s fame as a trumpeter is founded on two verses in 2 Samuel (ii.

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: Theodamas or Thiodamas, king of the Dryopes, plays a prominent part in the tenth book of Statius’ “Thebaid.”

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: Jongelours: jugglers; French, “jongleur.”

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: For explanation of this word, see note 14 to the Franklin’s tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: Pythonesses: women who, like the Pythia in Apollo’s temple at Delphi, were possessed with a spirit of divination or prophecy.

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: Subfumigations: a ceremony employed to drive away evil spirits by burning incense; the practice of smoking cattle, corn, &c., has not died out in some country districts.

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: In certain ascendents: under certain planetary influences.

scenes.title: Chapter 42
scenes.reentry: Medea: celebrated for her magical power, through which she restored to youth Aeson, the father of Jason; and caused the death of Jason’s wife, Creusa, by sending her a poisoned garment which consumed her to ashes.

scenes.title: Chapter 43
scenes.reentry: Circes: the sorceress Circe, who changed the companions of Ulysses into swine.

scenes.title: Chapter 44
scenes.reentry: Calypsa: Calypso, on whose island of Ogygia Ulysses was wrecked.

scenes.title: Chapter 45
scenes.reentry: Hermes Ballenus: this is supposed to mean Hermes Trismegistus (of whom see note 19 to the Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale); but the explanation of the word “Ballenus” is not quite obvious.

scenes.title: Chapter 46
scenes.reentry: Limote and Colle Tregetour seem to have been famous sorcerers or jugglers, but nothing is now known of either.

scenes.title: Chapter 47
scenes.reentry: Simon Magus: of whom we read in Acts viii.

scenes.title: Chapter 48
scenes.reentry: “And made well more than it was To seemen ev’rything, y-wis, As kindly thing of Fame it is;” i.e.

scenes.title: Chapter 49
scenes.reentry: Corbets: the corbels, or capitals of pillars in a Gothic building; they were often carved with fantastic figures and devices.

scenes.title: Chapter 50
scenes.reentry: A largess!: the cry with which heralds and pursuivants at a tournament acknowledged the gifts or largesses of the knights whose achievements they celebrated.

scenes.title: Chapter 51
scenes.reentry: Nobles: gold coins of exceptional fineness.

scenes.title: Chapter 52
scenes.reentry: Coat-armure: the sleeveless coat or “tabard,” on which the arms of the wearer or his lord were emblazoned.

scenes.title: Chapter 53
scenes.reentry: “But for to prove in alle wise As fine as ducat of Venise” i.e.

scenes.title: Chapter 54
scenes.reentry: Lapidaire: a treatise on precious stones.

scenes.title: Chapter 55
scenes.reentry: See imperial: a seat placed on the dais, or elevated portion of the hall at the upper end, where the lord and the honoured guests sat.

scenes.title: Chapter 56
scenes.reentry: The starres seven: Septentrion; the Great Bear or Northern Wain, which in this country appears to be at the top of heaven.

scenes.title: Chapter 57
scenes.reentry: The Apocalypse: The last book of the New Testament, also called Revelations.

scenes.title: Chapter 58
scenes.reentry: “Oundy” is the French “ondoye,” from “ondoyer,” to undulate or wave.

scenes.title: Chapter 59
scenes.reentry: Partridges’ wings: denoting swiftness.

scenes.title: Chapter 60
scenes.reentry: Hercules lost his life with the poisoned shirt of Nessus, sent to him by the jealous Dejanira.

scenes.title: Chapter 61
scenes.reentry: Of the secte Saturnine: Of the Saturnine school; so called because his history of the Jewish wars narrated many horrors, cruelties, and sufferings, over which Saturn was the presiding deity.

scenes.title: Chapter 62
scenes.reentry: Compare the account of the “bodies seven” given by the Canon’s Yeoman: “Sol gold is, and Luna silver we threpe; Mars iron, Mercury quicksilver we clepe; Saturnus lead, and Jupiter is tin, And Venus copper, by my father’s kin.”

scenes.title: Chapter 63
scenes.reentry: Statius is called a “Tholosan,” because by some, among them Dante, he was believed to have been a native of Tolosa, now Toulouse.

scenes.title: Chapter 64
scenes.reentry: Dares Phrygius and Dictys Cretensis were the names attached to histories of the Trojan War pretended to have been written immediately after the fall of Troy.

scenes.title: Chapter 65
scenes.reentry: Lollius: The unrecognisable author whom Chaucer professes to follow in his “Troilus and Cressida,” and who has been thought to mean Boccaccio.

scenes.title: Chapter 66
scenes.reentry: Guido de Colonna, or de Colempnis, was a native of Messina, who lived about the end of the thirteenth century, and wrote in Latin prose a history including the war of Troy.

scenes.title: Chapter 67
scenes.reentry: English Gaufrid: Geoffrey of Monmouth, who drew from Troy the original of the British race.

scenes.title: Chapter 68
scenes.reentry: Lucan, in his “Pharsalia,” a poem in ten books, recounted the incidents of the war between Caesar and Pompey.

scenes.title: Chapter 69
scenes.reentry: Claudian of Alexandria, “the most modern of the ancient poets,” lived some three centuries after Christ, and among other works wrote three books on “The Rape of Proserpine.”

scenes.title: Chapter 70
scenes.reentry: Triton was a son of Poseidon or Neptune, and represented usually as blowing a trumpet made of a conch or shell; he is therefore introduced by Chaucer as the squire of Aeolus.

scenes.title: Chapter 71
scenes.reentry: Sky: cloud; Anglo-Saxon, “scua;” Greek, “skia.”

scenes.title: Chapter 72
scenes.reentry: See note 5 to Chaucer’s Tale of Melibœus.

scenes.title: Chapter 73
scenes.reentry: Swart: black; German, “schwarz.”

scenes.title: Chapter 74
scenes.reentry: Tewell: the pipe, chimney, of the furnace; French “tuyau.”

scenes.title: Chapter 75
scenes.reentry: Tetches: blemishes, spots; French, “tache.”

scenes.title: Chapter 76
scenes.reentry: For the story of Belle Isaude see note 21 to the Assembly of Fowls.

scenes.title: Chapter 77
scenes.reentry: Quern: mill.

scenes.title: Chapter 78
scenes.reentry: To put an ape into one’s hood, upon his head, is to befool him; see the prologue to the Prioresses’s Tale, l.6.

scenes.title: Chapter 79
scenes.reentry: Obviously Chaucer should have said the temple of Diana, or Artemis (to whom, as Goddess of the Moon, the Egyptian Isis corresponded), at Ephesus.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The double sorrow: First his suffering before his love was successful; and then his grief after his lady had been separated from him, and had proved unfaithful.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: Tisiphone: one of the Eumenides, or Furies, who avenged on men in the next world the crimes committed on earth.

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: See Chaucer’s description of himself in “The House Of Fame,” and note 11 to that poem.

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: The Palladium, or image of Pallas (daughter of Triton and foster-sister of Athena), was said to have fallen from heaven at Troy, where Ilus was just beginning to found the city; and Ilus erected a sanctuary, in which it was preserved with great honour and care, since on its safety was supposed to depend the safety of the city.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: “Oh, very god!”: oh true divinity! — addressing Cressida.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
scenes.reentry: Ascaunce: as if to say — as much as to say.

scenes.title: Chapter 7
scenes.reentry: Eft: another reading is “oft.”

scenes.title: Chapter 8
scenes.reentry: Arten: constrain — Latin, “arceo.”

scenes.title: Chapter 9
scenes.reentry: The song is a translation of Petrarch’s 88th Sonnet, which opens thus: “S’amor non e, che dunque e quel ch’i’sento.”

scenes.title: Chapter 10
scenes.reentry: If maugre me: If (I burn) in spite of myself.

scenes.title: Chapter 11
scenes.reentry: The Third of May seems either to have possessed peculiar favour or significance with Chaucer personally, or to have had a special importance in connection with those May observances of which the poet so often speaks.

scenes.title: Chapter 12
scenes.reentry: Went: turning; from Anglo-Saxon, “wendan;” German, “wenden.”

scenes.title: Chapter 13
scenes.reentry: Procne, daughter of Pandion, king of Attica, was given to wife to Tereus in reward for his aid against an enemy; but Tereus dishonoured Philomela, Procne’s sister; and his wife, in revenge, served up to him the body of his own child by her.

scenes.title: Chapter 14
scenes.reentry: Fished fair: a proverbial phrase which probably may be best represented by the phrase “done great execution.”

scenes.title: Chapter 15
scenes.reentry: The fair gem virtueless: possessing none of the virtues which in the Middle Ages were universally believed to be inherent in precious stones.

scenes.title: Chapter 16
scenes.reentry: The crop and root: the most perfect example.

scenes.title: Chapter 17
scenes.reentry: Eme: uncle; the mother’s brother; still used in Lancashire.

scenes.title: Chapter 18
scenes.reentry: Dardanus: the mythical ancestor of the Trojans, after whom the gate is supposed to be called.

scenes.title: Chapter 19
scenes.reentry: All the other gates were secured with chains, for better defence against the besiegers.

scenes.title: Chapter 20
scenes.reentry: Happy day: good fortune; French, “bonheur;” both “happy day” and “happy hour” are borrowed from the astrological fiction about the influence of the time of birth.

scenes.title: Chapter 21
scenes.reentry: Horn, and nerve, and rind: The various layers or materials of the shield — called boagrion in the Iliad — which was made from the hide of the wild bull.

scenes.title: Chapter 23
scenes.reentry: Who gives me drink?: Who has given me a love-potion, to charm my heart thus away?

scenes.title: Chapter 24
scenes.reentry: That plaited she full oft in many a fold: She deliberated carefully, with many arguments this way and that.

scenes.title: Chapter 25
scenes.reentry: Through which I mighte stand in worse plight: in a worse position in the city; since she might through his anger lose the protection of his brother Hector.

scenes.title: Chapter 26
scenes.reentry: I am not religious: I am not in holy vows.

scenes.title: Chapter 27
scenes.reentry: The line recalls Milton’s “dark with excessive bright.”

scenes.title: Chapter 28
scenes.reentry: No weal is worth, that may no sorrow drien: the meaning is, that whosoever cannot endure sorrow deserves not happiness.

scenes.title: Chapter 29
scenes.reentry: French, “verre;” glass.

scenes.title: Chapter 30
scenes.reentry: From cast of stones ware him in the werre: let him beware of casting stones in battle.

scenes.title: Chapter 31
scenes.reentry: Westren: to west or wester — to decline towards the west; so Milton speaks of the morning star as sloping towards heaven’s descent “his westering wheel.”

scenes.title: Chapter 32
scenes.reentry: A pike with ass’s feet etc.: this is merely another version of the well-known example of incongruity that opens the “Ars Poetica” of Horace.

scenes.title: Chapter 33
scenes.reentry: Tristre: tryst; a preconcerted spot to which the beaters drove the game, and at which the sportsmen waited with their bows.

scenes.title: Chapter 34
scenes.reentry: A kankerdort: a condition or fit of perplexed anxiety; probably connected with the word “kink” meaning in sea phrase a twist in an rope — and, as a verb, to twist or entangle.

scenes.title: Chapter 35
scenes.reentry: They feel in times, with vapour etern: they feel in their seasons, by the emission of an eternal breath or inspiration (that God loves, &c.)

scenes.title: Chapter 36
scenes.reentry: The idea of this stanza is the same with that developed in the speech of Theseus at the close of The Knight’s Tale; and it is probably derived from the lines of Boethius, quoted in note 91 to that Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 37
scenes.reentry: In this and the following lines reappears the noble doctrine of the exalting and purifying influence of true love, advanced in “The Court of Love,” “The Cuckoo and the Nightingale,” &c.

scenes.title: Chapter 38
scenes.reentry: Weir: a trap or enclosed place in a stream, for catching fish.

scenes.title: Chapter 39
scenes.reentry: Nor might one word for shame to it say: nor could he answer one word for shame (at the stratagem that brought Cressida to implore his protection)

scenes.title: Chapter 40
scenes.reentry: “All n’ere he malapert, nor made avow Nor was so bold to sing a foole’s mass;” i.e. although he was not over-forward and made no confession (of his love), or was so bold as to be rash and ill-advised in his declarations of love and worship.

scenes.title: Chapter 41
scenes.reentry: Pandarus wept as if he would turn to water; so, in The Squire’s Tale, did Canace weep for the woes of the falcon.

scenes.title: Chapter 42
scenes.reentry: If I breake your defence: if I transgress in whatever you may forbid; French, “defendre,” to prohibit.

scenes.title: Chapter 43
scenes.reentry: These lines and the succeeding stanza are addressed to Pandarus, who had interposed some words of incitement to Cressida.

scenes.title: Chapter 44
scenes.reentry: In “The Court of Love,” the poet says of Avaunter, that “his ancestry of kin was to Lier; and the stanza in which that line occurs expresses precisely the same idea as in the text.

scenes.title: Chapter 45
scenes.reentry: 46.”Reheating” is read by preference for “richesse,” which stands in the older printed editions; though “richesse” certainly better represents the word used in the original of Boccaccio — “dovizia,” meaning abundance or wealth.

scenes.title: Chapter 47
scenes.reentry: “Depart it so, for widewhere is wist How that there is diversity requer’d Betwixte thinges like, as I have lear’d:” i.e. make this distinction, for it is universally known that there is a great difference between things that seem the same, as I have learned.

scenes.title: Chapter 48
scenes.reentry: Frepe: the set, or company; French, “frappe,” a stamp (on coins), a set (of moulds).

scenes.title: Chapter 49
scenes.reentry: To be “in the wind” of noisy magpies, or other birds that might spoil sport by alarming the game, was not less desirable than to be on the “lee-side” of the game itself, that the hunter’s presence might not be betrayed by the scent.

scenes.title: Chapter 50
scenes.reentry: Bothe fremd and tame: both foes and friends — literally, both wild and tame, the sporting metaphor being sustained.

scenes.title: Chapter 51
scenes.reentry: The lovers are supposed to say, that nothing is wanting but to know the time at which they should meet.

scenes.title: Chapter 52
scenes.reentry: A tale of Wade: see note 5 to the Merchant’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 53
scenes.reentry: Saturn, and Jove, in Cancer joined were: a conjunction that imported rain.

scenes.title: Chapter 54
scenes.reentry: Smoky rain: An admirably graphic description of dense rain.

scenes.title: Chapter 55
scenes.reentry: For the force of “cold,” see note 22 to the Nun’s Priest’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 56
scenes.reentry: Goddes seven: The divinities who gave their names to the seven planets, which, in association with the seven metals, are mentioned in The Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 57
scenes.reentry: Assayed: experienced, tasted.

scenes.title: Chapter 58
scenes.reentry: Now is it better than both two were lorn: better this happy issue, than that both two should be lost (through the sorrow of fruitless love).

scenes.title: Chapter 59
scenes.reentry: Made him such feast: French, “lui fit fete” — made holiday for him.

scenes.title: Chapter 60
scenes.reentry: The cock is called, in “The Assembly of Fowls,” “the horologe of thorpes lite;” [the clock of little villages] and in The Nun’s Priest’s Tale Chanticleer knew by nature each ascension of the equinoctial, and, when the sun had ascended fifteen degrees, “then crew he, that it might not be amended.”

scenes.title: Chapter 61
scenes.reentry: Fortuna Major: the planet Jupiter.

scenes.title: Chapter 62
scenes.reentry: When Jupiter visited Alcmena in the form of her husband Amphitryon, he is said to have prolonged the night to the length of three natural nights.

scenes.title: Chapter 63
scenes.reentry: Chaucer seems to confound Titan, the title of the sun, with Tithonus (or Tithon, as contracted in poetry), whose couch Aurora was wont to share.

scenes.title: Chapter 64
scenes.reentry: So, in “Locksley Hall,” Tennyson says that “a sorrow’s crown of sorrow is rememb’ring better things.”

scenes.title: Chapter 65
scenes.reentry: As great a craft is to keep weal as win: it needs as much skill to keep prosperity as to attain it.

scenes.title: Chapter 66
scenes.reentry: See the reference to Boethius in note 91 to the Knight’s Tale.

scenes.title: Chapter 67
scenes.reentry: The smalle beastes let he go beside: a charming touch, indicative of the noble and generous inspiration of his love.

scenes.title: Chapter 68
scenes.reentry: Mew: the cage or chamber in which hawks were kept and carefully tended during the moulting season.

scenes.title: Chapter 69
scenes.reentry: Love of steel: love as true as steel.

scenes.title: Chapter 70
scenes.reentry: Pandarus, as it repeatedly appears, was an unsucsessful lover.

scenes.title: Chapter 71
scenes.reentry: “Each for his virtue holden is full dear, Both heroner, and falcon for rivere”:That is, each is esteemed for a special virtue or faculty, as the large gerfalcon for the chase of heron, the smaller goshawk for the chase of river fowl.

scenes.title: Chapter 72
scenes.reentry: Zausis: An author of whom no record survives.

scenes.title: Chapter 73
scenes.reentry: And upon new case lieth new advice: new counsels must be adopted as new circumstances arise.

scenes.title: Chapter 74
scenes.reentry: Hid in mew: hidden in a place remote from the world — of which Pandarus thus betrays ignorance.

scenes.title: Chapter 75
scenes.reentry: The modern phrase “sixes and sevens,” means “in confusion:” but here the idea of gaming perhaps suits the sense better — “set the world upon a cast of the dice.”

scenes.title: Chapter 76
scenes.reentry: The controversy between those who maintained the doctrine of predestination and those who held that of free-will raged with no less animation at Chaucer’s day, and before it, than it has done in the subsequent five centuries; the Dominicans upholding the sterner creed, the Franciscans taking the other side.

scenes.title: Chapter 77
scenes.reentry: That have their top full high and smooth y-shore: that are eminent among the clergy, who wear the tonsure.

scenes.title: Chapter 78
scenes.reentry: Athamante: Athamas, son of Aeolus; who, seized with madness, under the wrath of Juno for his neglect of his wife Nephele, slew his son Learchus.

scenes.title: Chapter 79
scenes.reentry: Simois: one of the rivers of the Troad, flowing into the Xanthus.

scenes.title: Chapter 1
scenes.reentry: The birds on the weathervanes were set up facing the wind, so that it entered their open mouths, and by some mechanism produced the musical sound.

scenes.title: Chapter 2
scenes.reentry: “And to you been of governance Such as you found in whole pleasance” That is, “and have governed you in a manner which you have found wholly pleasant.”

scenes.title: Chapter 3
scenes.reentry: Hext: highest; from “high,” as “next” from “nigh.”

scenes.title: Chapter 4
scenes.reentry: “Your brother friend,” is the common reading; but the phrase has no apparent applicability; and perhaps the better reading is “our bother friend” — that is, the lady who has proved herself a friend both to me and to you.

scenes.title: Chapter 5
scenes.reentry: The ships had high embattled poops and forecastles, as in mediaeval ships of war.

scenes.title: Chapter 6
